days.title: Liveness, readiness, and startup probes
days.summary: Focus: Liveness, readiness, and startup probes

items.title: Liveness, readiness, and startup probes
items.body:
## Three questions the cluster asks your pod
A probe is the cluster periodically asking your container a yes/no question and acting on the answer. There are three, and the whole point is that they trigger different actions:
- **Liveness**: "are you still alive?" Fail it and Kubernetes restarts the container. This catches a process that is up but wedged, a deadlock, an event loop stuck forever.
- **Readiness**: "are you ready to serve traffic right now?" Fail it and the pod is pulled out of the Service's rotation, no traffic, but it is NOT restarted. This is for slow starts and temporary unavailability (warming a cache, running a migration).
- **Startup**: "have you finished starting?" It holds the liveness probe off until the app is up, so a slow boot is not mistaken for a deadlock.

```yaml
# inside the container spec
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 80 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 2
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 80 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
```

## The mistake that takes down a healthy app
The classic production incident is a liveness probe set too aggressive. You point liveness at `/healthz`, the endpoint occasionally takes 2 seconds under load, your `timeoutSeconds` is 1, so the probe fails, Kubernetes restarts the container, the restart drops in-flight requests and adds load, the next pod's probe times out too, and now the cluster is restarting healthy pods in a loop while traffic suffers. The rule that prevents it: liveness should test only "is the process fundamentally broken," nothing more. A liveness endpoint that touches the database or calls another service is a liveness probe that will kill your app the moment that dependency is briefly slow. Keep liveness dumb and local; put the real "can I serve" checks in readiness.

## Readiness is what gives you zero-downtime deploys
Readiness is the quiet hero of the rolling update from W9. During a deploy a new pod starts but its readiness probe fails until the app is actually up, so the Service keeps sending traffic only to the old pods. The instant the new pod reports ready it joins the rotation; only then does the old one get terminated. Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes assumes a pod is ready the moment the process starts and routes traffic to an app that is still booting, which is exactly the half-second of 502s users notice during a deploy.

## Where this fits
Add a `/healthz` route to your app that returns 200 when it is up, then wire readiness and liveness to it. Confirm with `kubectl describe pod` that the probes show as passing, then deliberately break `/healthz` and watch the pod drop out of the Service. Seeing the cluster react to your health signal is the point.

items.title: QoS classes
items.body:
## Requests and limits, and what each one actually does
Two numbers on a container, with very different jobs:
- **requests** is what the scheduler reserves. It only places the pod on a node with at least this much CPU and memory free. Set it too low and pods pile onto a node and fight; too high and you waste capacity.
- **limits** is the ceiling the pod may not cross. CPU and memory behave differently here, which trips everyone up once: exceed the **CPU** limit and the pod is **throttled** (slowed, but alive); exceed the **memory** limit and the pod is **OOMKilled** (terminated, then restarted). Memory has no "slow down" option, so a memory limit set below what your app really needs is a pod that dies under load.

```yaml
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
  limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }
```
`100m` is a tenth of a CPU core; `128Mi` is 128 mebibytes. The gap between requests and limits is your burst room: this pod is guaranteed a tenth of a core but may use up to half a core when the node has it spare.

## QoS is assigned, not chosen, and it decides who dies first
You never set a "QoS class." Kubernetes derives it from how you set requests and limits, and it decides which pods get evicted first when a node runs out of memory:
- **Guaranteed**: requests equal limits for every resource. Last to be evicted. Use it for anything that must not die.
- **Burstable**: requests set, limits higher or partial. Evicted after BestEffort. Most normal workloads land here.
- **BestEffort**: no requests or limits at all. First out the door when the node is under pressure.

So the practical lesson inverts how beginners treat it: setting requests and limits is not bureaucratic box-ticking, it is you telling the cluster how important this pod is. A pod with nothing set is a pod you have told Kubernetes it may kill first.

## The number you cannot guess from your laptop
Right-sizing requests is the part nobody gets right on the first try, and you cannot eyeball it. Run the app under realistic load and read actual usage with `kubectl top pod` (needs the metrics-server add-on). Set requests near steady-state usage and limits with headroom for spikes. Memory limits set too tight give you mystery OOMKills under load; too loose and one leaky pod takes down a node. This is tuning that only converges with real numbers, which is why production teams revisit it rather than set it once.

## Where this fits
Add requests and limits to your Edge Portfolio container so it lands in the Burstable class, then check the class with `kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -i qos`. You now control not just what your app needs, but where it sits in the queue when the cluster has to make hard choices.

items.title: PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim
items.body:
## Pods are disposable; some data is not
Everything in a pod's own filesystem vanishes when the pod dies, and pods die constantly: restarts, rescheduling, deploys. That is fine for your stateless web app, but the moment you run a database, a pod restart that wipes the data is a disaster. Kubernetes separates the lifecycle of storage from the lifecycle of pods with two objects:
- A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is an actual piece of storage in the cluster (a disk).
- A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a pod's request for storage: "I need 1Gi I can read and write." The PVC binds to a PV that satisfies it, and the pod mounts the PVC as a directory.

```yaml
# pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data }
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: { requests: { storage: 1Gi } }
```
```yaml
# in the pod spec
volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/data }]
volumes: [{ name: data, persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: data } }]
```

## You rarely create PVs by hand
You wrote a PVC but no PV, yet it binds. A **StorageClass** provisioned the PV the moment the claim appeared, which is how every cloud does it: on EKS the default StorageClass calls AWS and creates an EBS volume; on kind a local-path provisioner makes a directory on the node. This dynamic provisioning is why you almost never write a PV directly, you declare what you need (the PVC) and the StorageClass conjures the disk. Delete the pod, recreate it, and the PVC re-binds to the same disk: the data is still there.

## The access mode that surprises people
`ReadWriteOnce` (RWO) is the default and a common source of confusion. It does not mean "one pod ever." It means the volume can be mounted read-write by one **node** at a time. So a Deployment with 3 replicas all wanting the same RWO volume fails to schedule, because they may land on different nodes. RWO suits a single database pod; for many pods sharing one volume you need `ReadWriteMany` (RWX), which most block storage (like EBS) does not support, you reach for a networked filesystem (EFS, NFS). Most of the time the right answer is not "share a volume across pods," it is "give each stateful pod its own," which is exactly what tomorrow's StatefulSet does.

## Where this fits
Add a PVC, mount it in a pod, write a file into the mount, delete the pod, let it come back, and confirm the file is still there. That survival across a pod's death is the entire reason PVs exist, and it is what makes running stateful workloads on Kubernetes possible at all.

items.title: StatefulSets
items.body:
## A Deployment is the wrong shape for a database
A Deployment treats its pods as interchangeable: random name hashes, any pod replaceable by any other. That is perfect for your stateless web app and wrong for a database, where each replica has its own data and its own identity, the primary is not the same as a replica, and pod-2 must keep being pod-2 with pod-2's disk after a restart. The **StatefulSet** is the object for that, and it gives three things a Deployment will not:
- **Stable network identity**: pods are named `db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2`, not random hashes, and keep those names across restarts.
- **Stable per-pod storage**: each pod gets its own PVC (`data-db-0`, `data-db-1`), and `db-0` always re-binds to `data-db-0`.
- **Ordered rollout**: pods start and update one at a time, in order, which databases need for safe scaling and failover.

```yaml
# statefulset.yaml (abridged)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: db }
spec:
  serviceName: db                 # the headless Service that gives stable DNS
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: db } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: db } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: db
          image: postgres:16
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }]
  volumeClaimTemplates:           # one PVC PER pod, created automatically
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        resources: { requests: { storage: 1Gi } }
```

## The headless Service and why each pod gets a DNS name
A StatefulSet pairs with a **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`). Instead of load-balancing across pods like a normal Service, it gives each pod its own stable DNS name: `db-0.db`, `db-1.db`, `db-2.db`. That matters because with a database you often need to address a specific replica, your app writes to the primary `db-0` and reads from `db-1`. A normal Service hands you "some pod"; a headless Service lets you say which one.

## When NOT to reach for it
StatefulSets are harder to operate than Deployments, and the honest production advice is to avoid running your primary database on Kubernetes at all when a managed option exists. On AWS, RDS runs Postgres for you with backups, failover, and patching handled. A StatefulSet is the right tool for stateful workloads you must run in-cluster (Kafka, a cache cluster, a database you have a specific reason to self-host), not a default. Use it when you have decided, with eyes open, to own the operational burden.

## Where this fits
Run a 3-replica Postgres StatefulSet, watch `db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2` come up in order each with its own PVC, delete `db-1`, and confirm it returns as `db-1` re-bound to the same `data-db-1` disk. That stable identity-plus-storage is the thing a Deployment fundamentally cannot give you.

items.title: Graceful shutdown
items.body:
## A pod does not die instantly, and that matters
When Kubernetes terminates a pod (a deploy, a scale-down, a node drain), it does not yank it. It sends the container a **SIGTERM** signal, waits up to `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30), and only then sends SIGKILL. That window is your app's chance to finish what it was doing: stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests complete, close the database connection cleanly. An app that ignores SIGTERM and just gets killed drops every request it was mid-way through serving, which users see as random failures during every deploy.

## The handler your app needs
Your app has to actually catch SIGTERM and shut down on purpose. In Node:
```js
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(() => process.exit(0)); // stop new conns, finish in-flight, exit
});
```
Without that handler, the default behaviour is "die immediately on SIGTERM," and your careful Kubernetes config cannot save requests the app itself threw away. Graceful shutdown is a contract between two halves: Kubernetes gives you the window, your code has to use it.

## The race nobody expects: termination is concurrent
Here is the subtle part behind "I handle SIGTERM but still drop requests." When a pod is terminated, two things happen at the same time, not in sequence: the pod gets SIGTERM, AND it starts being removed from Service endpoints. Endpoint removal propagates through the cluster asynchronously, so for a brief moment a pod can be shutting down while still receiving new traffic. The standard fix is a `preStop` hook that sleeps a few seconds before SIGTERM, giving endpoint removal time to land first:
```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }
```
It looks like a hack and it is the recommended pattern: sleep, let the cluster stop sending you traffic, then shut down cleanly.

## Where this fits
Add the SIGTERM handler and the `preStop` sleep to your app, then do a rolling deploy while hitting the app with a steady stream of requests (a `while true; do curl ...; done` loop). With graceful shutdown done right, the deploy completes with zero failed requests. That zero is the whole deliverable of the day.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What "production-ready" means by tonight
This week's ship is proving your app behaves under conditions a demo never tests. Concretely, the `k8s/` folder now produces a Deployment that:
- has a readiness probe, so a rolling deploy serves zero errors;
- has a liveness probe dumb enough that it never restarts a healthy pod;
- has resource requests and limits, landing it in a known QoS class;
- handles SIGTERM with a `preStop` delay, so termination drops no requests.

## The test that proves it
Run the load test you could not run in W9. Start a steady request loop against the app's URL (`while true; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://edge.localdev.me; sleep 0.2; done`), then trigger a rolling deploy (`kubectl set image deployment/edge-portfolio web=youruser/edge-portfolio:1.1`). Watch the status codes. A pre-W10 deploy shows a burst of `502`/`000` as old pods die mid-request. A correctly hardened one shows an unbroken column of `200`. That difference, errors versus no errors during a deploy, is the entire point of the week made visible.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the updated `k8s/` folder and extend the README with the one thing that makes it credible: a sentence on each production field and why it is there ("readiness gates traffic so deploys are zero-downtime; liveness is intentionally local so a slow dependency cannot trigger a restart loop"). Anyone can copy a probe off the docs; explaining why yours are set the way they are is what shows you understand them.

## Where this fits in the track
You now run a stateless app to a production standard. Week 11 (Helm) stops you hand-editing this growing pile of YAML and turns it into a parameterised package; Week 14 moves it onto a real managed cluster on AWS. The probes, resources, and shutdown discipline you set here are not Kubernetes trivia, they are the same four concerns you configure on every platform you ever deploy to, just with different syntax.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a web application that takes 45 seconds to start (it runs database migrations on startup). You configure a liveness probe that checks /health every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3. What happens? The liveness probe starts immediately. After 30 seconds (3 failures × 10 seconds), Kubernetes determines the container is unhealthy and restarts it. The container restarts, takes another 45 seconds to start... and is killed again. This is a crash loop. The fix: add a startupProbe with failureThreshold: 60 and periodSeconds: 5 (total of 5 minutes for startup). The liveness probe is suspended until the startup probe succeeds. Once the app has started, liveness probe takes over.

weeks.title: Helm and the K8s Package Ecosystem
weeks.context:
Raw Kubernetes YAML is verbose, repetitive, and hard to manage across environments. A Deployment manifest for your staging environment is almost identical to production, but with different image tags, replica counts, resource limits, and environment variables. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes that solves this problem.

A Helm chart is a collection of templates and default values. Templates are Kubernetes YAML files with Go template syntax for parameterisation: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} is replaced with the value from values.yaml. You install a chart with helm install myrelease ./mychart --set image.tag=1.2.3. Helm renders the templates with the provided values and sends the resulting YAML to Kubernetes.

Charts have a standard directory structure: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, description), values.yaml (default values), templates/ (YAML templates), charts/ (chart dependencies). The values.yaml contains sensible defaults; users override them with --set or custom values files (helm install -f prod-values.yaml).

The Helm chart repository ecosystem: Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io) hosts thousands of community charts. Adding a repository: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami. Installing a chart: helm install my-postgres bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret. This is how you deploy PostgreSQL, Redis, nginx, Prometheus, and many other services without writing any YAML yourself.

Helm vs Kustomize: Helm uses Go templates for parameterisation (powerful but complex, logic, loops, conditionals). Kustomize uses overlays (patch files that override specific fields). Kustomize is simpler for small differences between environments; Helm is more powerful for complex parameterisation. Many teams use Kustomize for their own applications and Helm for third-party software (databases, monitoring stacks).

Helm release management: helm list shows installed releases. helm history myrelease shows the history of changes. helm rollback myrelease 2 rolls back to revision 2. helm uninstall myrelease removes all resources the release created.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
By now your `k8s/` folder is a pile of YAML: a Deployment, a Service, an Ingress, a ConfigMap, with probes and resource limits bolted on. It works, but it has two problems you are about to feel. Deploying the same app to dev and prod means copy-pasting that folder and hand-editing replica counts and image tags, which drifts the moment someone forgets. And installing something like Postgres means finding and maintaining a few hundred lines of YAML you did not write. This week you package your app as a **Helm chart**, one parameterised template you install into any environment with a single command, and you learn to pull battle-tested charts off the shelf for the software you should not be hand-writing.

## Why a package manager, not just more YAML
Helm is to Kubernetes what apt or npm is to their worlds: a way to install a named, versioned thing and its config in one command, and uninstall it just as cleanly. The shift it forces is from "a folder of YAML I apply" to "a chart I install as a release," and that release is a unit you can list, see the history of, and roll back. `helm rollback edge-portfolio 3` rewinds to a known-good revision in one line, which is a very different feeling from trying to remember what your YAML looked like last Tuesday.

## What stays the same
Helm does not replace anything you learned. Under the templating, it produces the exact same Deployment, Service, and Ingress objects you wrote by hand, and sends them to the same API server. If a Helm release misbehaves, you debug it with the same `kubectl describe` and `kubectl logs` as always. Helm is a layer that generates your YAML from a template plus values; it is not a new runtime. Keep that in mind and Helm stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like find-and-replace with structure.

## Where this fits
You convert your Edge Portfolio YAML into a chart this week, install it with different values for "dev" and "prod," and pull a community Postgres chart instead of writing one. Week 18's GitOps will deploy these charts automatically; for now the win is one template that serves every environment.

items.title: Helm fundamentals
items.body:
## A chart is templates plus values
A Helm chart is a folder with a fixed structure, and only three parts matter at first:
```text
edge-portfolio/
  Chart.yaml        # name, version, description of the chart itself
  values.yaml       # the default values (the knobs)
  templates/        # your K8s YAML, with {{ }} placeholders
```
The templates are your familiar Deployment and Service YAML, except the parts that change between installs become placeholders:
```yaml
# templates/deployment.yaml
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
```
```yaml
# values.yaml
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repo: youruser/edge-portfolio
  tag: "1.0"
```

## Install, upgrade, rollback: the three verbs
`helm install` renders the templates with the values, then sends the result to Kubernetes as a named release:
```bash
helm install edge ./edge-portfolio
helm upgrade edge ./edge-portfolio --set image.tag=1.1   # change one value
helm history edge        # every revision, with status
helm rollback edge 1     # back to revision 1, in one command
```
Each install or upgrade is a numbered revision. That history is the thing raw YAML never gave you: a record of what you deployed and a one-line undo.

## See what it renders before you ship it
The command that turns Helm from scary to obvious is `helm template`:
```bash
helm template edge ./edge-portfolio --set replicaCount=5
```
It renders the chart and prints the final YAML to your screen without touching the cluster. Run it whenever you are unsure what a template will produce, especially after editing a `{{ }}`. The number one Helm mistake is a templating error you only discover at install time; `helm template` (and `helm lint`) catches it on your laptop first. Read the rendered output, confirm it is the YAML you expect, then install.

## Where this fits
Convert your Edge Portfolio Deployment and Service into templates with a `values.yaml`, then `helm install` it and confirm with `kubectl get pods` that you get the same running app, now produced from a chart instead of hand-written YAML.

items.title: Values files for per-environment config (dev, staging, prod)
items.body:
## One chart, many environments, no copy-paste
The whole reason you packaged the app: the same chart should deploy to dev, staging, and prod with only the differences spelled out. You do that with per-environment values files that override the defaults in `values.yaml`:
```yaml
# values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 1
image: { tag: "dev" }
resources: { requests: { cpu: "50m", memory: "64Mi" } }
```
```yaml
# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 4
image: { tag: "1.2.0" }
resources: { requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" } }
```
```bash
helm install edge ./edge-portfolio -f values-prod.yaml
```
The base `values.yaml` holds sane defaults; each environment file says only what differs. Now "prod runs 4 replicas, dev runs 1" lives in one readable file instead of being buried in a forked copy of your YAML.

## Precedence: the rule that prevents surprises
When the same key is set in several places, Helm applies them in a fixed order, last wins: `values.yaml` first, then any `-f` file you pass, then any `--set` on the command line. So `helm install edge . -f values-prod.yaml --set replicaCount=6` runs 6 replicas, because the `--set` beats the file, which beats the default. Knowing this order is how you stop chasing "why did it use the wrong value," it is almost always a higher-precedence override you forgot about.

## Keep secrets out of values files
Values files get committed to git, so a real password in `values-prod.yaml` is a leaked password. The same rule from W9's Secrets applies here: environment-specific non-secret config goes in values files, but database passwords and API keys come from Kubernetes Secrets (or, in W16, a real secret manager), referenced by name in the template. A values file should be safe to show a stranger; if it is not, something sensitive is in the wrong place.

## Where this fits
Add `values-dev.yaml` and `values-prod.yaml`, install your chart twice into two namespaces with the two files, and confirm one runs a single small pod and the other runs four larger ones, from the same templates. That is the payoff of packaging: environments differ by a values file, not a forked folder.

items.title: Helm dependencies
items.body:
## Your app needs a database; do not write the database
Real apps depend on other software: a database, a cache, a message queue. Helm lets a chart declare those as **dependencies**, other charts it pulls in, so installing your app also stands up its Postgres. You declare them in `Chart.yaml`:
```yaml
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "15.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
```
```bash
helm dependency update ./edge-portfolio   # downloads the subchart into charts/
helm install edge ./edge-portfolio
```
Now one `helm install` brings up your app and a Postgres maintained by people who do databases for a living, instead of a StatefulSet you wrote and now have to keep patched.

## Configuring a subchart through your values
A dependency's own values are namespaced under its chart name in your `values.yaml`, so you configure Postgres without editing its chart:
```yaml
# values.yaml
postgresql:
  auth:
    database: edge
    username: edge
  primary:
    persistence:
      size: 2Gi
```
Everything under the `postgresql:` key is passed down to the Postgres subchart. This is the pattern that makes community charts usable: you never fork them, you override their values from your parent chart, and you re-pin the dependency version when you want their updates.

## The version pin is not optional
`version: "15.x.x"` pins which Postgres chart you depend on. Leave it loose and a `helm dependency update` six months from now silently pulls a major version with a breaking schema change, and your deploy fails in a way that is genuinely hard to trace. Pin dependency versions the same way you pin image tags by digest in W7: reproducibility means the same `helm install` gives the same result next year, and a floating dependency quietly breaks that promise.

## Where this fits
Add a Postgres dependency to your chart, configure it through your `values.yaml`, and bring up app-plus-database with one install. You now ship an application and its data layer as a single versioned unit, which is how real services are packaged.

items.title: Community charts
items.body:
## The thousands of charts you should be using
Most infrastructure you will run, Postgres, Redis, nginx, Prometheus, cert-manager, has a maintained Helm chart on Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io). Using one is three commands:
```bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm install cache bitnami/redis --set auth.password=secret
```
You just deployed a production-grade Redis, with persistence, metrics, and sane defaults, without writing or maintaining a line of its YAML. This is the largest practical leverage Helm gives you: the standard software you need has already been packaged by people who run it at scale, and reusing their work is the professional default, not a shortcut.

## Read the chart before you trust it
Convenience cuts both ways: `helm install` runs whatever the chart author put in the templates, in your cluster. Before installing something unfamiliar, two checks. Run `helm show values bitnami/redis` to read every knob and its default (especially anything about persistence, resources, and whether it exposes a service publicly). And prefer charts from a known publisher (Bitnami, or the project's own official chart) over a random one-star upload. A chart is code you are running with cluster permissions; treat an unknown one with the same suspicion you would an unknown npm package.

## Pin the version, always
`helm install cache bitnami/redis` grabs the latest chart version, which is fine for a one-off experiment and wrong for anything you will redeploy. Pass `--version` to pin it (`helm install cache bitnami/redis --version 19.0.1`), and record that version in your own chart's dependencies or your install scripts. The recurring theme of this whole track holds here too: an unpinned version is a future surprise, and "it worked last month" is not a deployment strategy.

## Where this fits
Replace the Postgres you might self-manage with a pinned community chart, install a second piece of infrastructure (Redis or nginx) from Artifact Hub, and read its values before doing so. Knowing when to pull a chart instead of writing YAML is a real seniority signal: most of an experienced operator's cluster is other people's well-chosen charts.

items.title: Alternatives
items.body:
## Helm is not the only way, and templating has a cost
Helm parameterises with Go templates, which are powerful (loops, conditionals, functions) and, past a point, hard to read: a heavily-templated chart becomes YAML buried under `{{ }}` you cannot eyeball anymore. **Kustomize** takes the opposite approach. Instead of templating, you keep plain, valid YAML and layer **overlays** that patch specific fields per environment:
```text
base/                   # plain Deployment + Service YAML (no placeholders)
overlays/
  prod/
    kustomization.yaml  # "use ../../base, then patch replicas to 4"
```
```bash
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod      # kustomize is built into kubectl
```
The base stays readable because it is real YAML you could apply directly; the overlay only describes the diff for prod.

## The honest split most teams land on
Neither tool wins outright, and the common production pattern uses both. Kustomize for your own apps, where the differences between environments are small and you value readable, template-free YAML. Helm for third-party software, where you want the packaging, dependencies, and one-command install of a maintained chart and you are not going to read its internals anyway. So "Helm vs Kustomize" is usually answered "Helm for what others wrote, Kustomize for what you wrote," and a real repo often has both.

## Why you learned Helm first anyway
You started with Helm because the ecosystem is in Helm: Artifact Hub, Bitnami, almost every piece of infrastructure you will install ships a chart, not a kustomization. You cannot avoid Helm. Kustomize is the lighter option you reach for once your own app's chart starts feeling over-templated, and knowing both means you can read any team's repo, since you will meet both in the wild within your first month on a real cluster.

## Where this fits
Re-express your app's per-environment config once as a Kustomize overlay alongside your Helm chart, and compare them. Feel which is more readable for your small dev-versus-prod diff. You are not picking a winner, you are learning to recognise which tool a problem is asking for.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app is now a Helm chart, not a folder of hand-edited YAML. By tonight:
- `helm install edge ./edge-portfolio -f values-prod.yaml` brings up the whole app from one parameterised template.
- the same chart with `values-dev.yaml` runs a smaller version, proving one template serves many environments.
- a pinned Postgres dependency comes up alongside it from one install.
- `helm history edge` shows your revisions, and `helm rollback` can undo a bad deploy in one line.

## The test that proves the packaging works
Do an upgrade-and-rollback round trip. `helm upgrade edge ./edge-portfolio --set image.tag=broken` to deploy a deliberately bad image, watch the pods fail, then `helm rollback edge 1` and watch the previous good revision come straight back. That one-command recovery is the concrete reason teams package apps as charts instead of applying loose YAML: a release has a history, and history means undo.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the chart: `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, the env value files, and a README that shows the install command for each environment and what each top-level value does. A reader should be able to `helm install` your app into their own cluster from the repo alone. The chart, not the running pods, is the portfolio piece; it is the thing that says you can package an application the way real teams ship them.

## Where this fits in the track
Your app is packaged and parameterised, which is the precondition for everything that follows. Week 18's Argo CD will watch a git repo and helm-deploy these charts automatically (GitOps); Week 14 installs them on a real EKS cluster. Hand-applying YAML was the right way to learn the objects; packaging them as a chart is how you stop doing it by hand for the rest of the track.

weeks.title: Service Mesh and Modern Networking, Istio, Linkerd, eBPF
weeks.context:
Kubernetes networking handles communication between pods and between the cluster and the outside world. But as applications grow more complex, microservices communicating with each other, diverse clients with different requirements, security policies between services, the basic Service and Ingress are not enough. Service meshes and modern networking tools fill this gap.

The service mesh problem: you have 50 microservices talking to each other. You want: mutual TLS (mTLS) between services (so a compromised service cannot spy on other services' traffic), traffic metrics (how many requests per second between service A and service B, what is the error rate), circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to a service that is failing), and gradual traffic shifting (send 5% of traffic to the new version before committing). Implementing all of this in each service's application code is duplicative and error-prone. A service mesh adds this as infrastructure, transparent to the application.

Istio: the most feature-rich service mesh. It injects a sidecar proxy (Envoy) into every pod. The sidecar intercepts all traffic in and out of the pod. Istio's control plane (istiod) configures the sidecars. From the application's perspective, nothing changes, it still makes HTTP requests to the Service. The sidecars handle mTLS, telemetry, and traffic policies transparently. The tradeoff: Istio is complex, resource-intensive (each sidecar adds ~50MB memory), and has a learning curve.

Linkerd: a lighter-weight service mesh focused on simplicity. Uses its own proxy (written in Rust, much lighter than Envoy). Provides mTLS, traffic metrics, and retries out of the box. Less feature-rich than Istio but significantly simpler to operate. The right choice if you want the core service mesh benefits without Istio's complexity.

eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter): a technology that allows you to run programs in the Linux kernel without modifying the kernel source or loading kernel modules. Cilium uses eBPF for Kubernetes networking: it replaces kube-proxy, provides high-performance networking, and can implement network policies and observability at the kernel level, without sidecar proxies. Cilium + Hubble (Cilium's observability component) provides service mesh-like capabilities without the sidecar overhead.

Kubernetes Ingress vs Gateway API: an Ingress routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to services. The Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor, it separates concerns between the infrastructure admin (Gateway), the cluster operator (Routes), and the developer (HTTPRoute). The Gateway API is the future of Kubernetes external traffic management.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Everything so far assumed one app. Real systems are dozens of services calling each other, and that fan-out creates problems a Service and an Ingress do not solve: how do you encrypt traffic between services so a single compromised pod cannot read everyone else's data, how do you see the request rate and error rate between service A and service B, how do you shift 5% of traffic to a new version before trusting it, and how do you stop hammering a service that is already failing? This week is the layer that answers those, the **service mesh**. You will run one (Linkerd, the simpler one), put your app behind it, and watch it add mTLS and per-service metrics without you changing a line of application code.

## Why this is more "understand" than "build"
Be honest with yourself about this week's altitude. A service mesh is most of the time the wrong tool for a small system, and you may not run one for years. The goal here is not to make you a mesh operator; it is so that when an architecture diagram has "Istio" on it, or someone proposes adding a mesh, you understand what problem it solves, what it costs, and when the answer should be "not yet." That judgement is the deliverable, more than any YAML.

## The one idea under all of it: the sidecar
Almost every service mesh works the same way: it injects a second container, a **sidecar proxy**, into each of your pods, and quietly reroutes all traffic in and out through that proxy. Your app still thinks it is making a plain HTTP call to a Service; the proxy is what actually adds the encryption, the metrics, and the retries. That is the trick that makes a mesh "transparent to the application", the new behaviour lives in the proxy beside your app, not in your code. Hold that picture and Istio, Linkerd, and the eBPF alternatives all become variations on one theme.

## Where this fits
You install Linkerd, mesh your Edge Portfolio app, and see mTLS and a live traffic dashboard appear for free. Then you spend the week understanding the tradeoffs, because knowing when not to add this layer is worth more than knowing how to add it.

days.title: What a service mesh is
days.summary: Focus: What a service mesh is

items.title: What a service mesh is
items.body:
## The four things a mesh gives you, and why not to code them yourself
A service mesh moves four cross-cutting concerns out of your application and into infrastructure:
- **mTLS**: every service-to-service call is mutually authenticated and encrypted, so a pod that gets compromised cannot silently read traffic between other services.
- **Telemetry**: a uniform request rate, error rate, and latency for every service-to-service hop, without each team instrumenting their code the same way.
- **Traffic control**: retries, timeouts, and circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to a failing service) applied as policy.
- **Traffic shifting**: send 5% of requests to a new version, watch its error rate, then ramp, a canary at the network layer.

The reason this belongs in a mesh and not in each service: implementing all four correctly in every service, in every language your company uses, is duplicated, inconsistent, error-prone work. The mesh does it once, the same way, for everything.

## How the sidecar actually intercepts traffic
When you mesh a namespace, the mesh injects an Envoy or Linkerd proxy container into each pod and rewrites the pod's network rules so all inbound and outbound traffic goes through that proxy first. Your app calls `http://payments` exactly as before; the local proxy catches the call, opens an mTLS connection to the payments pod's proxy, records the metrics, and forwards it. Neither app knows the proxy is there. The control plane (istiod for Istio, the Linkerd control plane for Linkerd) is the brain that pushes config and certificates to all those proxies.

## The cost you are buying
This is not free, and the price is concrete. Every pod now runs a second container, so you add memory and CPU per pod (Istio's Envoy sidecar is roughly 50MB of memory each, multiplied by every pod). Every request now makes two extra proxy hops, adding a little latency. And you have a whole new control plane to operate, upgrade, and debug, and mesh failures are confusing precisely because the mesh is invisible to the app. Whether those four benefits are worth this is the entire "do we need a mesh" decision, and for a handful of services the answer is usually no.

## Where this fits
Install Linkerd, mesh your app's namespace, and run `linkerd viz dashboard` to see live mTLS and per-route metrics that you did not write any code to produce. Then look at the sidecar with `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'`, there are now two containers where you defined one. Seeing that injected proxy is seeing the whole mechanism.

items.title: Traffic splitting and canary deploys at the mesh level
items.body:
## A canary the network does for you
W9 to W11 gave you rolling deploys: replace old pods with new ones, gated by readiness. A mesh gives you something finer, a **canary by traffic percentage**. You run both versions at once and tell the mesh to send, say, 5% of requests to v2 and 95% to v1, watch v2's error rate and latency on the mesh dashboard, and only shift more traffic when it looks healthy. If v2 misbehaves, you shift back to 0% instantly, no pod restarts, no rollback deploy, just a routing change.

## What it looks like
With Linkerd or Istio you express the split as a routing rule. The shape (Istio here) is:
```yaml
# 95% to v1, 5% to v2
http:
  - route:
      - destination: { host: edge, subset: v1 }
        weight: 95
      - destination: { host: edge, subset: v2 }
        weight: 5
```
Bump the weights toward v2 over minutes or hours as the metrics hold, and you have a progressive rollout decoupled from deployment. The new version is deployed the whole time; how much real traffic it sees is a dial you turn, watching the error rate the mesh is already collecting for you.

## Why this beats a plain rolling update for risky changes
A rolling update is all-or-nothing per pod: once a new pod is ready it serves 100% of its share, and if the bug only shows under real traffic you find out after it is fully rolled out. A 5% canary limits the blast radius of a bad release to 5% of users and gives you a metric-driven gate before the other 95% is exposed. This is how teams ship a change to a payment path or a recommendation model without betting the whole service on it, and tools like Flagger (W17) automate the "watch the metrics, ramp if healthy, roll back if not" loop on top of the mesh.

## Where this fits
Deploy a v2 of your app, define a traffic split sending it a small slice, and watch the mesh dashboard show requests flowing to both versions with separate success rates. Shift the weight and watch traffic move in real time. You are decoupling "is it deployed" from "how many users see it," which is the core idea behind every safe-rollout strategy in the rest of the track.

items.title: Linkerd vs Istio
items.body:
## Two answers to the same problem, very different weights
Istio and Linkerd both give you mTLS, metrics, and traffic control via sidecars; they differ mostly in power versus simplicity.
- **Istio** is the feature-rich one. Its Envoy sidecar supports almost any traffic-management scenario you can name, and it integrates with everything. The cost is real complexity: more moving parts, a heavier sidecar (~50MB/pod), and a genuine learning curve. Istio is what large platform teams run when they need its full surface.
- **Linkerd** is the deliberately-simple one. Its proxy is written in Rust, is much lighter, and the project's whole philosophy is "do the core mesh things, do them with sane defaults, stay easy to operate." It has mTLS, metrics, and retries working out of the box with very little config. It does less than Istio on purpose.

## How to actually choose
The honest decision rule is not "which is better" but "how much do you need." If you want the core benefits, encrypted service traffic and golden metrics, with the least operational burden, Linkerd is the default, and most teams that think they need Istio would be better served by Linkerd. You reach for Istio when you have a specific requirement only its richer feature set or ecosystem integrations satisfy, and a platform team that can carry its complexity. Choosing the heavier tool because it is more famous is how teams end up operating a mesh more complex than the system it runs on.

## The third option you already met
Remember from D1 that not every mesh uses sidecars. The eBPF approach (tomorrow's topic, Cilium) provides much of this at the kernel level with no per-pod proxy, which sidesteps the memory and latency cost entirely. So the real menu is three-way: Istio (most features, most weight), Linkerd (core features, light), and eBPF/Cilium (kernel-level, no sidecar). Knowing all three exist is what lets you push back when someone reaches for the heaviest option by reflex.

## Where this fits
You ran Linkerd this week precisely because it gets you a working mesh fastest. Spend today reading the Istio "what is a sidecar" docs and comparing the two install experiences so the difference is concrete, not abstract. The skill is being able to say, in a design discussion, why a small team should start with Linkerd and what specific need would justify Istio.

items.title: eBPF
items.body:
## Running your code inside the kernel, safely
**eBPF** (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is the technology under the newest networking tools, and the one-sentence version is: it lets you run small, sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel without writing a kernel module or recompiling the kernel. Because networking, security, and observability ultimately happen in the kernel, eBPF lets tools hook in at that level, seeing and shaping every packet, with far less overhead than doing the same work up in user space.

## Why this matters for Kubernetes: no sidecar
The headline application is **Cilium**, an eBPF-based networking layer for Kubernetes. Because it works in the kernel, it can do things the sidecar meshes do, network policy, load balancing, mTLS, deep observability, without injecting a proxy into every pod. That directly attacks the cost you learned about in D2: no per-pod 50MB sidecar, no extra proxy hop of latency, because the kernel itself is doing the interception. Cilium can replace `kube-proxy` entirely, and its companion **Hubble** gives you a live service-dependency map and flow visibility that feels like a mesh dashboard, again with no sidecars.

## The honest state of it
eBPF is genuinely where cluster networking is heading, and it is also less mature and more demanding than the sidecar meshes for the full set of mesh features. The practical read: a lot of clusters already run Cilium as their plain networking layer (CNI) and benefit from its performance and observability without calling it a "mesh." Reaching for its more advanced service-mesh capabilities is a newer, more specialised choice. You do not need to deploy Cilium this week; you need to understand that "service mesh" no longer automatically means "sidecar," and that the kernel-level approach is where the heavy parts of this space are moving.

## Where this fits
This is a read-and-understand day, not a build day, and that is the right call for a kernel-level technology you will not operate as a beginner. Watch a short Cilium/Hubble demo and note one thing: the dependency graph it draws between services is the same picture a mesh gives you, produced without a single sidecar. Knowing that distinction is what keeps you current in a conversation about modern cluster networking.

days.title: When NOT to use a service mesh
days.summary: Focus: When NOT to use a service mesh

items.title: When NOT to use a service mesh
items.body:
## The most valuable thing in this week is a "no"
Most teams that adopt a service mesh did it too early, and paid for it in complexity they did not need. So the senior move is knowing the conditions under which a mesh is not worth it:
- **You have a handful of services.** mTLS, fine-grained traffic control, and per-hop metrics solve problems of scale. With five services, the mesh is more operational surface than the system it secures.
- **You can get the one thing you actually want more cheaply.** Often the real need is just "encrypt traffic between services" or "see request metrics." mTLS can come from your CNI (Cilium) or app-level TLS; metrics can come from your app and Prometheus (W19). If one need drives the decision, solve that need directly.
- **You do not have someone to operate it.** A mesh is a distributed system you now run in addition to your app. Adding it without the team capacity to upgrade, debug, and reason about it trades a problem you understand for one you do not.

## The trap: complexity that outweighs the system
A mesh adds a control plane, a sidecar per pod, and a new failure mode where the mesh itself is what is broken, with confusing symptoms because the mesh is invisible to the app. For a small system, that added complexity can easily exceed the complexity of the services it is managing, which is the exact opposite of what infrastructure is supposed to do. The question to ask out loud is not "would a mesh help" (it usually would, a little) but "does the benefit clear the operational cost for a system this size."

## When the answer flips to yes
To be fair to the tool: a mesh earns its keep when you genuinely have many services, multiple teams, a real requirement for zero-trust mTLS everywhere, or a need for fine-grained progressive delivery across services. At that scale, hand-rolling the four concerns from D2 across dozens of services is worse than running a mesh. The skill is recognising which side of that line your system is on, and most beginners' systems are nowhere near it.

## Where this fits
Write, for your own Edge Portfolio, the honest one-paragraph answer: does it need a mesh? (It does not, and being able to say why clearly is the point.) Carrying a default of "probably not yet, here is what would change my mind" into your first job will save a team from a self-inflicted wound, because someone will propose adding a mesh, and a clear-eyed reason to wait is genuinely valuable.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
This week's deliverable is mostly understanding, plus one running mesh. By tonight:
- Linkerd is installed and your app's namespace is meshed, with mTLS active between pods you did not configure by hand.
- `linkerd viz dashboard` shows live success rate and latency per route, metrics you wrote no code to produce.
- you have a written, honest assessment of whether your own app should run a mesh (it should not), with the specific conditions that would change that.

## Prove the mesh is actually doing something
Make the invisible visible. Run `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'` and see two containers where your chart defines one, that second one is the injected proxy. Then check `linkerd viz edges deployment` to see the mTLS-secured connections between your workloads. Being able to point at the sidecar and the encrypted edges is how you demonstrate you understand what the mesh added, rather than just that you ran an install command.

## Ship the judgement, not just the install
The portfolio artifact for this week is unusual: a short written decision. In your repo's README or a `docs/mesh.md`, write what a service mesh provides, what it costs, and your reasoned call on whether this system needs one. A paragraph that says "we evaluated Linkerd, here is what it would give us and what it would cost, and here is why we are not adopting it yet" is a more senior signal than any amount of YAML, because it shows you can resist adding infrastructure for its own sake.

## Where this fits in the track
You now understand the layer above basic Kubernetes networking, and crucially, when to leave it alone. The traffic-shifting idea from D3 returns in Week 17 as Flagger-driven progressive delivery; the observability the mesh hinted at becomes Week 19's Prometheus and Grafana built deliberately. The mesh was your first look at treating cross-service concerns as infrastructure, a theme the rest of the cloud and SRE weeks keep building on.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Explain how Istio's mutual TLS (mTLS) works between two services without changing the application code. When service A wants to talk to service B, A's application code makes an HTTP request to B's Service DNS name. The Envoy sidecar in A's pod intercepts the outgoing request. It looks up the certificate for service B from istiod (Citadel, the Istio CA). It upgrades the connection to TLS, presents A's certificate to B's sidecar, and verifies B's certificate. B's sidecar verifies A's certificate and forwards the decrypted request to the service B application. The application never sees TLS, it makes plain HTTP internally. From outside the pod, all traffic is encrypted and authenticated.

weeks.title: Terraform, Infrastructure as Code Done Right
weeks.context:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means your infrastructure is defined in version-controlled files, just like your application code. Before IaC: you click through a cloud console to create a VPC, subnets, security groups, EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers. The configuration exists only in the cloud provider's database. There is no record of why you made each decision. Recreating it in another region takes hours and is error-prone. After IaC with Terraform: your entire infrastructure is in .tf files. Recreating it is terraform apply. Auditing is git blame.

Terraform is the dominant IaC tool. It uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), a declarative syntax that describes desired infrastructure state. Providers connect Terraform to cloud APIs: AWS, GCP, Azure, Cloudflare, GitHub, Datadog, and hundreds more. Terraform talks to the provider APIs to create, update, and delete resources.

The Terraform workflow. terraform init: downloads providers and modules. terraform plan: shows what changes will be made (resources to create, update, or destroy) without making them. Always review the plan. terraform apply: makes the changes. terraform destroy: tears down all resources. The plan/apply separation is Terraform's safety net, you see what will happen before it happens.

State: Terraform maintains a state file (terraform.tfstate) that maps your configuration to real cloud resources. The state is how Terraform knows what exists and what needs to change. Problem: the state file contains sensitive values (database passwords, API keys) and must be stored securely and shared across team members. Solution: remote state in S3 (with DynamoDB for state locking) or Terraform Cloud. Never commit terraform.tfstate to git.

Modules: reusable Terraform configurations. A module encapsulates a set of resources and exposes input variables and output values. The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) has community modules for common patterns: VPCs, EKS clusters, RDS instances. Instead of writing 200 lines of AWS VPC configuration, use the terraform-aws-vpc module with a few variables.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS**, use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Azure**, substitute **LocalStack** / local tooling; the concepts transfer directly.
- **Monitoring**, use **Prometheus + Grafana** locally (free).

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You met Terraform in Week 1, enough to stand up an S3 bucket and a CloudFront distribution. This week you use it the way teams actually do: remote state so more than one person can run it safely, modules so you stop copy-pasting resource blocks, and data sources so your config reads real values out of AWS instead of you hardcoding them. The concrete target is the cloud foundation your app will run on, a VPC with public and private subnets, defined as reusable Terraform, with its state living in S3 and locked so two applies can never corrupt it. Next week that foundation is where your EKS cluster lands.

## Why "Terraform done right" is its own week
The gap between "I can `terraform apply` a bucket" and "I can own a team's infrastructure" is not more resources, it is three habits: never letting state live only on your laptop, never repeating yourself, and never hardcoding a value you could look up. Skip those and Terraform scales into a 2,000-line `main.tf` that one person understands and everyone else is afraid to touch. This week is about the structure that keeps infrastructure code maintainable past the first month.

## The one rule that matters most: protect the state
Terraform's state file is the map between your code and the real resources it created, and it is the single most dangerous file in the repo. It holds secrets in plain text, and if two people apply at once they can corrupt it and leave your infrastructure in a state Terraform can no longer reason about. Today's non-negotiable, the thing every other lesson this week assumes, is remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking. Get that wrong and nothing else you do safely scales to a second person.

## Where this fits
You build a VPC module and wire up remote state this week, the groundwork for W14's EKS cluster and W16's secrets. By Sunday `terraform apply` from a clean checkout reproduces your network foundation, and the state that proves what exists lives in S3, not on any one machine.

items.title: Modules
items.body:
## Stop copy-pasting resource blocks
The second time you write a VPC, you notice it is the same forty lines as the first, with three values changed. A module is the fix: a folder of Terraform that takes inputs and produces resources, called like a function. Your root config stops being a wall of resources and becomes a short list of module calls:
```hcl
module "network" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
  cidr   = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs    = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
  env    = "prod"
}
```
The module defines its inputs with `variable` and what it returns with `output`, exactly the seam from yesterday, now used to package a whole network you can call twice with different values.

## You will mostly use other people's modules
The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) has battle-tested modules for the things everyone builds. A production-grade AWS VPC is hundreds of lines of subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and internet gateways done correctly; the `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` module gives you all of it for a dozen inputs:
```hcl
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "5.x.x"
  name    = "edge"
  cidr    = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs             = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24"]
  enable_nat_gateway = true
}
```
Writing that VPC by hand to the same quality would take a day and a few subtle bugs. This is the same leverage as W11's Helm charts: the standard infrastructure is already packaged, and using it well is the professional default.

## Pin the version, read what it makes
Two habits with registry modules, both familiar by now. Pin `version` so a future `terraform init` cannot pull a breaking major release into your infrastructure. And run `terraform plan` and actually read what the module will create before you apply, a VPC module quietly stands up NAT gateways that cost real money per hour, and "I didn't know it made those" is a bad way to find out on the bill. A module is convenient, not magic; you are still responsible for what it provisions.

## Where this fits
Wrap your network in the community VPC module (or your own), pinned and planned, and call it from your root config. Your infrastructure is now composed of named, reusable pieces instead of one long file, which is what makes W14's EKS module drop in cleanly on top.

items.title: Data sources
items.body:
## Read from the cloud instead of hardcoding
A resource creates something; a data source reads something that already exists. The difference matters more than it sounds, because hardcoding values AWS already knows is how configs rot. The classic example is an AMI (the base image for an EC2 instance): its ID changes every time AWS publishes a new build, so hardcoding `ami-0abc123` means your config is stale within weeks. A data source looks it up live:
```hcl
data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["099720109477"] # Canonical
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-22.04-*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id   # always the current Ubuntu 22.04
}
```

## Wiring configs together without copy-paste
Data sources also let one config read another's outputs instead of you pasting IDs between files. Your app config needs the VPC and subnets from your network config; rather than hardcoding their IDs, read them from the network's remote state:
```hcl
data "terraform_remote_state" "network" {
  backend = "s3"
  config = {
    bucket = "edge-tfstate-yourname"
    key    = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-east-1"
  }
}

# use it:
subnet_ids = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.private_subnet_ids
```
Now if the network changes, the app config picks up the new values automatically. This is how teams split infrastructure into separate, independently-applied configs that still know about each other, the seam that keeps a large estate from becoming one terrifying apply.

## The mental rule
The line to internalise: if a value lives in the cloud or in another config, read it with a data source; do not paste it. Hardcoded IDs are a config that is correct today and wrong after the next change someone else makes. Data sources keep your infrastructure honest by deriving values at plan time instead of freezing them in the file.

## Where this fits
Replace a hardcoded AMI or subnet ID with a data source, and read your network's outputs via `terraform_remote_state`. Your configs now compose by looking each other up, which is exactly how W14's cluster config will consume this week's network without you copying a single ID.

items.title: Workspaces vs separate state files
items.body:
## Two ways to run the same config for dev and prod
You have one VPC module; you need a dev environment and a prod environment from it. Terraform offers two patterns, and choosing wrong causes real pain later. Workspaces keep one config and one backend but switch between named state files (`terraform workspace new prod`); your code branches on `terraform.workspace`. Separate state files (usually separate directories or backend keys per environment) keep dev and prod fully isolated, each with its own state, its own backend key, applied independently.

## Why most teams avoid workspaces for environments
Workspaces look tempting (one command to switch) but carry a sharp risk: dev and prod share the same code path and the same backend, and it is genuinely easy to run `terraform apply` thinking you are on dev while the workspace is set to prod. There is no strong wall between them. The pattern that scales is separate state per environment, a `prod/` and `dev/` that each call the shared module with their own values and their own backend key:
```text
live/
  prod/   -> backend key network/prod, calls ../../modules/vpc with prod inputs
  dev/    -> backend key network/dev,  calls ../../modules/vpc with dev inputs
modules/
  vpc/    -> the shared module, written once
```
The module is shared (no duplication); the state and the apply are isolated (no cross-environment accident).

## When workspaces are the right tool
To be fair to workspaces, they are not useless, they are just mis-applied to environments. They fit ephemeral, identical copies of the same thing: a per-pull-request preview environment, a short-lived test stack you spin up and tear down. There the isolation risk is low and the "one command, new copy" ergonomics are exactly right. The rule of thumb: workspaces for many identical throwaway copies, separate state for long-lived environments you must never confuse.

## Where this fits
Lay out a `live/dev` and `live/prod` that both call your VPC module with different inputs and different backend keys. You now have a structure where promoting a change to prod is deliberate and isolated, not a workspace you hope you remembered to switch.

items.title: Terragrunt and Atmos
items.body:
## The repetition Terraform leaves you with
Yesterday's separate-state layout is the right pattern, and it has a cost you will feel quickly: every `live/<env>` directory repeats the same backend block, the same provider config, the same module-call boilerplate, with a few values changed. Terraform itself has no clean way to share that wiring across environments. Terragrunt is a thin wrapper built to fix exactly this. It keeps your backend and provider configuration in one root file and generates it into each environment, so a new environment is a short `terragrunt.hcl` with just its inputs:
```hcl
# live/prod/network/terragrunt.hcl
include "root" { path = find_in_parent_folders() }   # shared backend + provider
terraform { source = "../../../modules/vpc" }
inputs = { cidr = "10.0.0.0/16", env = "prod" }
```
The backend block you wrote ten times collapses to one, and `terragrunt run-all apply` can apply a whole environment in dependency order.

## Atmos and the broader point
Atmos (by Cloud Posse) solves the same DRY-environments problem with a different philosophy: configuration in YAML, strong conventions, "stacks" that compose components. You do not need to learn it deeply today; you need to know it exists and what category it is in. Both Terragrunt and Atmos answer one question, "how do I run Terraform across many environments without copy-pasting the wiring," and a real company at scale uses one of them (or an in-house equivalent) rather than raw Terraform across dozens of directories.

## Whether you need this yet
Be honest about altitude: for your Edge Portfolio with two environments, raw Terraform with a `dev/` and `prod/` is completely fine, and adding Terragrunt now is solving a problem you do not have. The value of today is recognition, not adoption. When you join a team and see `terragrunt.hcl` files everywhere, you will understand they are not exotic, they are the standard answer to keeping many environments DRY. Reach for these tools when the copy-paste between environments starts to actually hurt, not before.

## Where this fits
Read a Terragrunt example and map it onto yesterday's `live/` layout so the connection is concrete. You are not required to convert your project; you are building the vocabulary to read the infrastructure repos you will actually meet, where raw Terraform is often wrapped by one of these.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your cloud foundation now exists as real, reviewable Terraform. By tonight:
- a VPC (public and private subnets across two AZs) stands up from a module, called by a `live/` environment directory.
- state lives in S3, encrypted, with DynamoDB locking, not on your laptop.
- the config reads what it can with data sources instead of hardcoding IDs.
- `terraform plan` from a clean checkout shows "no changes," the proof that your code and reality match.

## The test that proves it
Run the IaC version of W9's destroy-and-rebuild. From a clean clone, `terraform init` (it pulls state from S3) then `terraform plan`: a correct setup reports no changes, because the state in S3 already reflects what your code describes. Then change one input (an extra subnet), `plan`, and read the diff: exactly one resource to add, nothing destroyed. Being able to predict the plan from the code, and have the plan match, is what "infrastructure as code" actually buys you, no surprises at apply time.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the `modules/` and `live/` directories with a README that states the one thing a reader needs: how to run it (`terraform init && terraform plan` against the S3 backend) and the fact that `terraform.tfstate` is deliberately NOT in the repo (it is in S3). Add the `.gitignore` for `*.tfstate` and `.terraform/`. The repo plus the S3 state, together, are a complete, reproducible description of your network.

## Where this fits in the track
You have the network foundation and the Terraform discipline (remote state, modules, data sources, isolated environments) that the rest of the cloud phase stands on. Next week the `terraform-aws-eks` module drops onto this VPC to give you a real managed Kubernetes cluster; Week 16 adds secrets management; Weeks 17 and 18 automate the applies. Clicking infrastructure together was never the job; capturing it as code others can review and rebuild is.

items.body: You change the instance_type of an existing EC2 instance in your Terraform configuration from t3.micro to t3.small. You run terraform plan. What does the plan show, and what happens to the running instance? Terraform shows: "aws_instance.web will be updated in-place" with instance_type changing from t3.micro to t3.small. weeks.title: Managed Kubernetes, EKS, GKE, AKS
weeks.context:
Managed Kubernetes services (EKS on AWS, GKE on Google Cloud, AKS on Azure) eliminate the burden of managing the Kubernetes control plane. In a self-managed cluster, you are responsible for: etcd backups, API server certificate rotation, control plane version upgrades, master node high availability, and more. With a managed service, the cloud provider handles all of that. You pay for the worker nodes; the control plane is managed.

EKS (Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service): AWS manages the control plane. You provision worker nodes (EC2 instances) in node groups, or use Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage, pods run directly). EKS integrates with AWS services: IAM for authentication (IRSA, IAM Roles for Service Accounts, letting pods assume IAM roles without long-lived credentials), ALB (Application Load Balancer) for Ingress, EBS/EFS for PersistentVolumes.

GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine): Google's managed Kubernetes. Often regarded as the most polished managed Kubernetes experience, GKE invented the technology after all. Features: Autopilot mode (GKE manages both control plane and nodes, fully managed), binary authorisation (only signed container images can run), and seamless integration with Cloud Run for serverless workloads.

AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service): Microsoft's offering. Strong integration with Azure Active Directory for authentication and Azure Monitor for observability. Popular in enterprise environments where Microsoft products dominate.

eksctl is the official CLI for EKS: eksctl create cluster --name myapp --region us-east-1 creates a complete EKS cluster. For production, use Terraform (terraform-aws-eks module) to manage the cluster as IaC. The eksctl approach is good for learning; Terraform is right for production.

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): the secure way to give Kubernetes pods access to AWS services. Instead of mounting long-lived AWS credentials into pods (security risk), IRSA lets pods assume an IAM role via a Kubernetes Service Account. The mechanism: an OIDC identity provider in your EKS cluster, an IAM role with a trust policy that allows the service account, and an annotation on the Kubernetes Service Account. Pods in that service account automatically receive temporary credentials for the IAM role.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Until now your Kubernetes lived on kind, a throwaway cluster on your laptop. This week it becomes real: a managed EKS cluster on AWS, sitting on the VPC you built in Terraform last week, running the same app from the same YAML and Helm charts you already wrote. The point of "managed" is that AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane (the API server, etcd, the scheduler) for you, and you only own the worker nodes your pods run on. By Sunday your Edge Portfolio is serving from EKS behind a real AWS load balancer, provisioned as Terraform, and you understand what that managed control plane is doing and what it costs.

## Why managed, and why this is mostly the same Kubernetes
The reason nobody self-runs the control plane in production is the list of chores it removes: etcd backups, API server certificate rotation, control-plane upgrades, master high-availability. EKS does all of that; you pay an hourly fee for the control plane and for your worker nodes. Crucially, the Kubernetes you learned does not change. The same Deployment, Service, Ingress, probes, and Helm charts from W9 to W12 apply unchanged. What is new is the seam between Kubernetes and AWS: how a pod authenticates to AWS, how an Ingress becomes a real load balancer, how a PersistentVolume becomes an EBS disk.

## The one genuinely new idea: pods that are AWS identities
The most important new concept this week is IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). On kind, a pod needing AWS access was a non-question. On EKS, the wrong answer is to bake AWS keys into the image, a credential that leaks and never expires. IRSA is the right answer: a pod assumes an AWS IAM role through its Kubernetes Service Account and gets temporary, auto-rotating credentials, with no long-lived secret anywhere. It is fiddly the first time and it is the thing that separates a toy cluster from one you would run a company on, so most of D3 is spent making it click.

## Where this fits
You stand up EKS with the `terraform-aws-eks` module on last week's VPC, deploy your app to it, and expose it through an AWS load balancer. This is the week your local Kubernetes practice becomes a cloud deployment, on infrastructure you can rebuild from code.

items.title: Managed K8s comparison
items.body:
## Same Kubernetes, three landlords
EKS (AWS), GKE (Google), and AKS (Azure) are the same Kubernetes with different operators and different integration points. Your manifests are portable across all three; what differs is the surrounding cloud:
- **EKS** integrates deeply with AWS: IAM for auth, ALB for Ingress, EBS/EFS for storage. It is the default if your company is on AWS, and it asks you to wire more of the integration yourself than the others.
- **GKE** is widely regarded as the most polished managed Kubernetes, unsurprising since Google created Kubernetes. Its Autopilot mode manages the nodes too, so you hand over even more operational burden.
- **AKS** is Microsoft's, strong on Azure Active Directory auth and Azure Monitor, and common in enterprises already standardised on Microsoft.

## The choice is almost never about Kubernetes
The honest decision rule: you do not pick a managed Kubernetes on its Kubernetes features, because they are nearly the same. You pick the one that matches the cloud your company already uses, because the value is in the integration with that cloud's IAM, networking, storage, and billing. A team on AWS runs EKS not because EKS is best in the abstract but because their identities, their VPCs, and their bill already live in AWS. Portability of your manifests is real insurance, but day to day you optimise for fitting the cloud you are in.

## What "managed" still leaves you holding
Managed does not mean hands-off. On EKS you still own the worker nodes (their size, scaling, and patching unless you use Fargate), the cluster's networking and security configuration, and the integration glue (IRSA, the load balancer controller, the storage driver). GKE Autopilot takes more of that; EKS takes less. Knowing exactly where the provider's responsibility ends and yours begins, the shared-responsibility line, is what stops you assuming AWS is handling something it is not.

## Where this fits
You are using EKS because this track is on AWS and your VPC is already there. Spend today understanding the comparison so the choice is informed, not defaulted, and so you can read a cloud-agnostic claim critically: your YAML is portable, your cluster's AWS integration is not.

items.title: AWS-specific integrations
items.body:
## Where Kubernetes meets AWS
A bare EKS cluster runs pods, but the value is in three integrations that connect Kubernetes objects to AWS services. Each replaces something that was free on kind with something real on AWS:
- **IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) gives a pod an AWS identity.
- The **AWS Load Balancer Controller** turns a Kubernetes Ingress into a real ALB.
- The **EBS CSI driver** turns a PersistentVolumeClaim into a real EBS disk.

## IRSA, the one to actually understand
This is the security-critical one. The wrong way to give a pod AWS access is to put an access key in a Secret or the image, a long-lived credential that leaks and never rotates. IRSA wires it up properly through four pieces: your cluster has an OIDC identity provider; you create an IAM role whose trust policy says "this specific Kubernetes Service Account may assume me"; you annotate the Service Account with the role ARN; and pods using that Service Account automatically receive temporary AWS credentials.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: edge-app
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/edge-app-s3-read
```
A pod under this Service Account can read its S3 bucket with no key anywhere, and the credentials expire and refresh on their own. That is the difference between a credential you have to rotate and one you never have to think about.

## ALB and EBS, the other two
The AWS Load Balancer Controller watches for Ingress objects and provisions an Application Load Balancer to match, so the Ingress you wrote in W9 now resolves to a real, public AWS endpoint instead of a local one. The EBS CSI driver makes the PVCs from W10 bind to actual EBS volumes, so a StatefulSet's storage is durable AWS storage. The pattern is the same in all three: an in-cluster controller you install once watches Kubernetes objects and creates the matching AWS resource. Your manifests stay standard Kubernetes; the controllers translate them into AWS.

## Where this fits
Set up IRSA for your app's Service Account and install the load balancer controller so your Ingress gets a real ALB. When your pod reads from S3 with no credentials in sight, and your URL resolves through an AWS load balancer, you have connected Kubernetes to AWS the way production does, which is most of what makes EKS more than "kind in the cloud."
