items.title: Cluster autoscaling
items.body:
## Two different things people call "autoscaling"
EKS scales at two levels, and confusing them is a common mistake. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA, from W10) adds more pods when your app is busy. Cluster autoscaling adds more nodes when there is no room to place those pods. They work together: HPA wants three more pods, the nodes are full, so the cluster autoscaler adds a node for them to land on; when load drops, pods scale down and the autoscaler removes the now-empty node so you stop paying for it.

## Karpenter, the modern answer
The older tool is the Cluster Autoscaler, which scales fixed node groups. The newer, increasingly default one on EKS is Karpenter, which is smarter: instead of scaling predefined groups, it looks at the pending pods, figures out the cheapest mix of instance types that would fit them, launches exactly that, then consolidates underused nodes to cut waste. The practical effect is better bin-packing and a smaller bill, because you are not paying for half-empty fixed-size nodes.
```text
pending pods need 6 vCPU, 12GB
Karpenter -> launches one right-sized Spot node that fits them
load drops -> Karpenter drains and removes it
```

## Why this is a money lesson as much as a scaling one
Node autoscaling is where Kubernetes cost discipline lives. A cluster with no autoscaling is either over-provisioned (you pay for idle nodes) or fragile (no room for spikes). Done right, it tracks demand: scale out for the spike, scale in afterward, and use Spot instances for workloads that tolerate interruption to cut node cost by a large margin. This connects straight to W21 (FinOps), where most Kubernetes overspend turns out to be idle node capacity an autoscaler would have removed.

## Where this fits
Enable node autoscaling (Karpenter or the Cluster Autoscaler) on your EKS cluster, then scale your Deployment up past what the current nodes can hold and watch a new node appear to accommodate the pods, then disappear when you scale back down. Seeing capacity follow demand automatically is the point, and it is what makes a cluster both elastic and affordable.

items.title: Multi-tenancy
items.body:
## Sharing one cluster without teams stepping on each other
A real company does not give every team its own cluster, that is expensive and hard to operate. It shares clusters, which raises the question this day answers: how do you let multiple teams or environments run on one cluster without them interfering? The first tool is namespaces, the logical partition you have used since W9, now doing real work, each team gets a namespace as its boundary. On top of namespaces you layer three controls that turn a soft boundary into a real one.

## The three controls that make a namespace a wall
- **ResourceQuotas** cap how much CPU and memory a namespace can consume in total, so one team cannot starve the cluster.
- **RBAC** (Role-Based Access Control) scopes what each team can do, team A can deploy in namespace A and nowhere else.
- **NetworkPolicies** control which pods can talk to which, so namespace A's services cannot reach namespace B's database unless you allow it.
Together these turn "we all share a cluster" from a hope into an enforced boundary. Without them, "we share a cluster" just means several teams sharing one blast radius and hoping for the best.

## Soft vs hard multi-tenancy, and the honest limit
There is a ceiling worth knowing. Namespaces plus quotas plus RBAC plus network policies give you soft multi-tenancy, fine for teams within one company who are not actively hostile. They do not give you hard multi-tenancy, safe isolation between untrusted parties, because tenants still share the same kernel and control plane, and a serious container escape crosses namespace lines. If you genuinely need to isolate untrusted workloads (a SaaS running customers' arbitrary code), the answer is separate clusters or stronger sandboxing, not namespaces. Knowing that line keeps you from over-trusting a namespace boundary.

## Where this fits
Carve your cluster into namespaces with a ResourceQuota and a basic NetworkPolicy, and scope a role to one namespace. You are practising the controls that let real clusters host many teams safely, and learning exactly how far that safety extends, which is the judgement that matters when someone proposes putting untrusted workloads on a shared cluster.

items.title: Cost
items.body:
## EKS has a bill, and it has a shape
Managed Kubernetes is not free, and the cost has predictable parts. The EKS control plane is a flat hourly charge per cluster (about $0.10/hour, roughly $73/month) no matter how small, which is why running five tiny clusters costs more than one shared cluster. Then you pay for worker nodes (EC2), usually the largest line; for any load balancers your Ingresses create; for EBS volumes; and for data transfer (especially cross-AZ traffic, an easy surprise). Knowing the shape tells you where to look when the bill is too high: almost always the nodes.

## The levers that actually move the bill
Three changes do most of the saving, and you have met all of them:
- **Right-size and autoscale nodes** so you are not paying for idle capacity, the single biggest source of Kubernetes waste (W4's lever, now at cluster scale).
- **Use Spot instances** for interruption-tolerant workloads (batch jobs, stateless web pods behind several replicas), often a large discount over on-demand; Karpenter makes this easy.
- **Consolidate clusters.** Because the control plane is a flat per-cluster fee, a few well-shared clusters beat many small ones. This is the cost argument for the multi-tenancy you set up yesterday.

## Avoid the cluster that costs money doing nothing
The trap with a learning cluster is leaving it running. An idle EKS cluster still bills the control plane, the nodes, the NAT gateway from your VPC, and any load balancers, which can be tens of dollars a week for something you are not using. The discipline, and a real production one, is that infrastructure you are not using should not exist: tear the cluster down with `terraform destroy` when you are done for the week and rebuild it with `terraform apply` next session. Because it is all IaC, that round trip is cheap and safe, which is one more reason last week's Terraform mattered.

## Where this fits
Look at the cost breakdown of your own cluster (AWS Cost Explorer, or just reason through the parts), then practise the most important habit, `terraform destroy` it when the week's work is done. Treating a cluster as something you stand up and tear down on demand, rather than a pet you leave running, is both the cost lesson and the reason you built it as code.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app now runs on real managed Kubernetes. By tonight:
- an EKS cluster, provisioned by the `terraform-aws-eks` module on last week's VPC, is running.
- your Edge Portfolio is deployed to it from the same Helm chart you wrote in W11, unchanged.
- it is reachable through a real AWS load balancer created from your Ingress by the load balancer controller.
- your app's pod reads AWS with IRSA, with no long-lived credentials anywhere.

## The test that proves it
Two checks. First, portability: the manifests and chart you deploy to EKS are the same ones that ran on kind, so prove it by pointing `kubectl` at EKS and applying the identical chart with a prod values file. If it comes up, you have shown your Kubernetes work was never tied to one environment. Second, IRSA: exec into your pod and run an AWS CLI command against its allowed service (`aws s3 ls` on its bucket); it should succeed with no credentials configured, because IRSA handed it temporary ones. A pod doing AWS work with no key in sight is the moment EKS stops being "kind in the cloud."

## Ship the artifact, then tear it down
Commit the EKS Terraform and the prod Helm values with a README that covers two things: the command to stand the whole thing up (`terraform apply` then `helm install`), and an explicit note that the cluster is meant to be destroyed when idle (`terraform destroy`) because it costs real money. Then actually destroy it. The deliverable is the code that can recreate a production-grade cluster on demand, not a running cluster you are quietly paying for all month.

## Where this fits in the track
You have taken the entire Kubernetes stack from a laptop to a managed cloud cluster, on infrastructure defined as code, with cloud-native identity and load balancing. Week 16 adds real secrets management to it; Weeks 17 and 18 stop you deploying by hand and make a git push do it. The big shift of this phase is complete: your app is not running on your machine anymore, it is running on infrastructure you can describe, rebuild, and hand to someone else.

weeks.title: Multi-Cloud, Vendor Lock-in, and Picking Your Platform
weeks.context:
Every cloud provider has different APIs, different pricing models, different service names, and different strengths. AWS has the broadest service catalogue. GCP has the best Kubernetes and data engineering services. Azure is dominant in enterprise environments with Microsoft licenses. Choosing a cloud provider (or using multiple) is a significant architectural decision.

Vendor lock-in is the state where you depend on a specific vendor's proprietary services to the point where switching is prohibitively expensive. The opposite of lock-in is portability, running the same workload on any cloud or on-premises. The tension: proprietary managed services (AWS Lambda, GCP BigQuery, Azure Cosmos DB) offer significantly better developer experience and operational leverage than self-managed open source equivalents, but they tie you to a vendor.

The lock-in spectrum. High lock-in: using AWS Lambda (serverless, AWS-specific), DynamoDB (NoSQL, AWS-specific), SageMaker (ML platform). Low lock-in: running containerised applications on Kubernetes (portable across managed Kubernetes services and on-premises), PostgreSQL (runs everywhere), S3-compatible object storage (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2). The pragmatic approach: use proprietary services where the operational leverage is worth the lock-in. Avoid proprietary services for core data storage where migration cost is highest.

Multi-cloud: running workloads across multiple cloud providers simultaneously. The reasons: regulatory requirements (data must stay in a specific region where only one provider has a data centre), avoiding single-vendor risk, negotiating leverage. The reality: multi-cloud adds significant operational complexity. Most startup and mid-size companies do not need multi-cloud. If you are using Kubernetes, you are already 80% of the way to cloud-portable, the remaining 20% is storage, networking, and cloud-specific services.

Cloud-native vs cloud-agnostic: cloud-native means using the managed services of a specific cloud to their fullest extent (Lambda + DynamoDB + SQS + SNS + RDS + ...). Cloud-agnostic means running only portable workloads (containers on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Redis) that could run on any cloud. The pragmatic answer for most teams: be cloud-native for your chosen cloud (pick one and use it well) and accept the lock-in as a reasonable operational tradeoff.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You committed to AWS for this whole track, and that was the right call. This week steps back to ask the question that decision implies: how tied to AWS are you, how much should you care, and what would it actually take to leave? This is a thinking week more than a building one. You will inventory exactly which parts of your stack are portable and which are AWS-only, look at the tools that promise cloud-agnosticism (and what they cost), deploy one thing to a completely different provider, and come out able to make the lock-in tradeoff deliberately instead of by accident.

## Why lock-in is a tradeoff, not a sin
The internet is full of warnings about vendor lock-in, and most are too simple. Proprietary managed services (Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS) genuinely give you more leverage than self-hosting the open-source equivalent, and that leverage is worth real money in saved operational time. The cost is that leaving gets expensive. So lock-in is not a mistake to avoid at all costs; it is a price you pay for convenience, and the skill is knowing when the convenience is worth it (almost always, for compute) and when the switching cost is too dangerous (usually, for your core data store).

## The reassuring part: you are already mostly portable
Here is the thing that makes this week less scary than the lock-in scolds suggest. By building on Kubernetes, containers, and PostgreSQL, you are already about 80% cloud-portable, your app, its packaging, and its database run on any cloud. The lock-in that actually bites is concentrated in the remaining 20%: cloud-specific storage, networking, IAM, and the proprietary services you choose to lean on. Knowing the portable core is already handled lets you spend your worry budget where it counts.

## Where this fits
You will catalogue your own stack's lock-in, try one genuinely different platform, and write a one-page rationale for your cloud choice. This is the week your AWS commitment goes from a default you fell into to a decision you can defend, which is exactly what a senior engineer is expected to do.

items.title: Plan before you build

items.title: Lock-in inventory
items.body:
## Put your own stack on the lock-in spectrum
The abstract debate gets useful the moment you grade your own components. Lock-in is a spectrum, not a yes/no, so go through your Edge Portfolio stack and place each piece:
- **Low lock-in (portable):** your containers and Kubernetes manifests (run on any managed K8s or on-prem), PostgreSQL (runs everywhere), S3-compatible object storage (AWS S3, but also Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, MinIO).
- **High lock-in (AWS-specific):** IAM and IRSA, the ALB and its controller, EKS-specific glue, and anything you reach for like DynamoDB, Lambda, or SQS.

## The asymmetry that should guide you
The inventory reveals a rule worth internalising: lock-in cost is highest for data and lowest for compute. Moving stateless compute between clouds is mostly re-pointing a deploy, annoying, not existential. Moving a database, with its data, its schema, and every app that depends on its exact dialect, is a genuine project. So the pragmatic stance falls out naturally: accept lock-in freely for compute and managed conveniences, and be deliberately conservative about proprietary data stores, where the migration bill is the one that can sink a project. Using DynamoDB is a reversible-ish decision; making it your system of record is much less so.

## How to record it so it is useful later
An inventory is only worth doing if your future self can act on it. For each component, note three things: how locked-in it is, what the portable alternative would be, and a rough sense of what switching would cost. "Object storage: AWS S3, alt is R2/MinIO, switching cost low (S3-compatible API)" is an entry that tells a future you exactly how exposed that choice is. The document is not academic, when someone proposes a second cloud or a big AWS price hike lands, this inventory is what turns panic into a ranked list of what is easy and what is hard to move.

## Where this fits
Build the inventory for your own stack and rank the entries by switching cost. You now hold a concrete map of your AWS exposure rather than a vague worry about lock-in, which is the input to every decision the rest of the week makes.

items.title: Cloud-agnostic abstractions (Crossplane, Pulumi) and their cost
items.body:
## The tools that promise "write once, run on any cloud"
A category of tools promises to abstract the cloud away so you are not locked in. Two worth knowing. Pulumi is infrastructure as code, like Terraform, but in real programming languages (TypeScript, Python, Go) instead of HCL; it still targets each cloud's API, but lets you wrap multi-cloud logic in code you already write. Crossplane goes further: it turns infrastructure provisioning into Kubernetes itself, you define a cloud database as a Kubernetes custom resource and Crossplane's controllers reconcile it into a real RDS (or Cloud SQL) instance, the same desired-state model you learned for pods, applied to cloud resources.

## The cost the marketing skips
These tools are genuinely useful, and they do not make lock-in disappear, they move it. Two costs are real. First, the abstraction is leaky: clouds differ in ways no common layer fully hides (an RDS instance and a Cloud SQL instance are not the same shape), so the "agnostic" config still sprouts cloud-specific branches. Second, you have traded vendor lock-in for tool lock-in, your whole infrastructure now depends on Crossplane or Pulumi, their concepts, their failure modes, their upgrade path. You did not remove a dependency; you added one and hoped it is a friendlier landlord.

## When they earn their place, and when they do not
The honest read: a cloud-agnostic layer pays off when you genuinely operate across multiple clouds, or sell software customers run on their own cloud of choice, real multi-cloud, where the abstraction's cost buys you something you need. For a single-cloud team (you, and most companies), adopting Crossplane to "avoid lock-in" you are not actually suffering is adding complexity to solve a hypothetical. Terraform targeting AWS directly is simpler and clearer than Crossplane abstracting a cloud you are never going to leave. Reach for these when multi-cloud is a real requirement, not a fear.

## Where this fits
Read a Crossplane or Pulumi example and map it against the Terraform you wrote in W13, feel where the abstraction helps and where it just adds a layer. You are not adopting either today; you are learning to recognise when an "agnostic" tool solves a real problem versus selling insurance against one you do not have.

items.title: Cloudflare Workers + Pages
items.body:
## A genuinely different shape of cloud
Everything so far has been the big-three model: rent VMs and managed services in a region. Cloudflare is a different philosophy worth feeling firsthand. Pages hosts static sites and front-ends on Cloudflare's global edge (a natural home for the static Edge Portfolio you started with). Workers run your code at the edge too, in hundreds of cities, starting in milliseconds with no server or region to manage, and R2 is S3-compatible object storage with no egress fees, a pointed jab at AWS's data-transfer bill. The model is "deploy a function to the whole planet" rather than "rent a box in us-east-1."

## What it is great at, and what it is not
Edge platforms shine for a specific shape: globally-distributed, latency-sensitive, request/response work, an API, a static site, light personalisation, things that benefit from running close to every user and scaling to zero between requests. They are a poor fit for others: long-running processes, heavy stateful workloads, anything needing a traditional always-on server or a large in-region database. Workers also run a constrained runtime (not full Node.js), so not every library works. Knowing the shape keeps you from forcing a workload onto the edge that wants a normal server, or the reverse.

## Why deploy here this week
Deploying one thing to Cloudflare is the fastest way to feel how different "cloud" can be, and to make your lock-in inventory concrete. Putting your portfolio's front-end on Pages takes minutes and costs nothing, and it proves a point from D2: the portable parts of your stack really are portable, you just moved a front-end to a completely different provider with no AWS involved. R2 also gives you a real, free answer to one specific AWS pain (egress fees), a tangible example of using a second provider for one job without going full multi-cloud.

## Where this fits
Deploy your portfolio's static front-end to Cloudflare Pages, and read how Workers and R2 work. You have now touched a fundamentally different cloud model, which both broadens what "pick a platform" means and demonstrates, hands-on, that the portable layer of your stack is not chained to AWS.

items.title: Pricing comparison
items.body:
## Cloud pricing is deliberately hard to compare
Comparing cloud costs is harder than it should be, and that is partly on purpose, every provider names and meters things differently so a clean apples-to-apples is rarely possible. But a few structural truths cut through. Compute (VMs, per vCPU-hour) is broadly comparable across the big three. The places they differ sharply, and where bills get surprising, are the edges: data egress (moving data OUT of the cloud is expensive on AWS/GCP/Azure and free on Cloudflare R2), inter-AZ and inter-region transfer, managed-service premiums, and the support plan. The headline VM price is the part everyone quotes and rarely the part that decides the bill.

## The cost that ambushes people
The single most common billing surprise is data transfer, especially egress. A workload that looks cheap on the compute line can run up a large transfer bill if it serves a lot of data to users or shuffles data across zones. This is why R2's "no egress fees" is a real differentiator and not just marketing, and why a multi-cloud setup can be quietly expensive (data crossing between clouds is egress on both sides). When you estimate a cloud's cost, model the data movement, not just the instances, that is where the gap between providers, and between a naive estimate and the real invoice, actually lives.

## How to compare without fooling yourself
Two habits make a cloud cost comparison honest. First, price the whole workload, compute plus storage plus transfer plus managed services plus support, not just the VM, because the non-compute lines are where providers diverge. Second, use each provider's own calculator with realistic numbers and assume the real bill runs higher than the estimate (calculators omit the small line items that add up). And remember the comparison is rarely decisive on its own: a 10% price difference almost never justifies the operational cost of switching clouds, which is why "pick one and use it well" usually beats "chase the cheapest provider."

## Where this fits
Estimate your Edge Portfolio stack's monthly cost on AWS, then sketch what the same thing would cost elsewhere, paying attention to transfer and managed-service lines. You are learning to reason about cloud cost structurally, which feeds directly into D6's "which platform for your stage" decision and into the FinOps work in W21.

items.title: Choosing for your stage
items.body:
## The right cloud depends on where you are, not what is best
There is no universally correct cloud, only the right one for your stage and situation, and the honest decision rules are unglamorous:
- **Solo or early startup:** pick one provider and go deep, optimise for shipping speed, not theoretical portability. What kills you at this stage is moving slowly, not lock-in. Often the right pick is simply the cloud you (or your team) already know.
- **Growth-stage:** you start caring about cost structure and a few specific managed services' strengths; you might add a second provider for one job (R2 for egress, a specialised ML service) without going multi-cloud.
- **Enterprise / regulated:** the drivers change entirely, data-residency law, existing Microsoft or Google agreements, procurement, and avoiding single-vendor risk can outweigh any technical preference.

## Match the provider to your real constraints
The choice should fall out of your actual constraints, not a benchmark. AWS for the breadth of services and the largest talent pool. GCP if Kubernetes and data/ML are central and you value the most polished managed K8s. Azure if your company lives in Microsoft licensing and Active Directory. Cloudflare for edge-first, globally-distributed, cost-sensitive web workloads. The mistake is picking on a feature comparison in the abstract; the right move is naming your top two or three constraints (team skills, the one service you depend on, your compliance reality) and letting those pick the cloud.

## Why "boring and one" usually wins
For almost everyone reading this, the correct answer is unexciting: choose one cloud and use it well. Multi-cloud's operational tax, two of everything, data egress between them, double the expertise, is real and rarely repaid except under genuine regulatory or scale pressure. Being cloud-native on one provider, and accepting that lock-in as a deliberate, reasonable tradeoff, beats being half-portable on two. The confidence to commit to one cloud, and to say why, is itself the senior signal here.

## Where this fits
Write the one-paragraph decision for your own project: which cloud, and the two or three constraints that pick it. You are practising the exact reasoning a team lead does when standing up a new system, turning "we use AWS because we always have" into "we use AWS because of X, Y, Z, and here is what would change our mind."

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
This week's deliverable is judgement, made concrete. By tonight:
- a lock-in inventory of your stack, each component graded portable vs cloud-specific, ranked by switching cost.
- one thing actually deployed to a non-AWS provider (your front-end on Cloudflare Pages), proving the portable layer is portable.
- a one-page cloud-choice rationale: which provider, and the specific constraints that justify it.

## The artifact that shows seniority
The portfolio piece here is unusual and valuable: a written architectural decision. Put a `docs/cloud-strategy.md` in your repo that states your cloud choice, the lock-in inventory behind it, and your reasoning, including what would make you reconsider. This is exactly the kind of document a senior engineer writes and a hiring manager looks for, because it shows you can weigh tradeoffs and commit, rather than either cargo-culting "avoid lock-in" or grabbing the newest service with no thought for the exit. Anyone can list cloud features; reasoning about lock-in in writing is rarer.

## Prove the portability claim, do not just assert it
Back the inventory with the one concrete demo: your front-end running on Cloudflare with no AWS in the path. That single deploy converts "my stack is mostly portable" from a claim into a thing you did, and it is the honest test of the D2 inventory, the components you graded "low lock-in" should actually move with little effort, and now one of them has.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now reason about cloud platforms and lock-in like an architect, which closes out the cloud-strategy thread of this phase. Next week (Secrets Management) returns to hands-on building on your chosen cloud, and the deliberate single-cloud commitment you made here is the backdrop for the CI/CD, GitOps, and observability work that follows. You stopped treating "which cloud" as an accident and made it a decision you own.

weeks.title: Secrets Management, Where Credentials Actually Live
weeks.context:
Secrets management is one of the most consequential security decisions in infrastructure. A secret is any value that provides access: API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys, OAuth client secrets, SSH private keys. How you store, distribute, rotate, and audit secrets determines whether a breach exposes just one system or your entire infrastructure.

The worst approach: hardcoded secrets in source code. They end up in git history forever, visible to everyone with repository access, and copied into every developer's machine. The second-worst: environment variables on servers set manually. They are visible in /proc/environ, are not rotated, and are not audited. Better: Kubernetes Secrets (base64-encoded, stored in etcd, accessible only to pods with the right RBAC). But Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default and are only as secure as your cluster's etcd access control.

HashiCorp Vault is the industry standard secret management solution. It provides: dynamic secrets (generate database credentials on-demand that expire after an hour, no static passwords), static secret storage (API keys you cannot make dynamic), secret leasing and renewal, fine-grained access control (AppRole, Kubernetes auth), and full audit trail (every secret access is logged). Vault's dynamic secrets for databases are transformative: instead of storing a password for your database, your application asks Vault for credentials at startup, Vault creates a short-lived PostgreSQL user, and your app uses it. When the credentials expire, Vault revokes the database user. No password to steal.

Cloud provider secret managers: AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault. These are managed equivalents of Vault, less feature-rich (no dynamic secrets for most sources) but operationally simpler and natively integrated with their cloud services. AWS Secrets Manager automatically rotates RDS passwords and integrates with ECS, Lambda, and EC2 via IAM. Use the cloud provider's secret manager for most use cases; consider Vault for complex multi-cloud or on-premises scenarios.

Secrets in Kubernetes: the External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or other backends into Kubernetes Secrets. Pods use the Kubernetes Secrets as normal; ESO handles fetching and rotation from the external store. This gives you the cloud secret manager's operational benefits while keeping the Kubernetes Secret as the delivery mechanism for pods.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS**, use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Azure**, substitute **LocalStack** / local tooling; the concepts transfer directly.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

## Context
This applies specifically to week 16 ('Secrets Management, Where Credentials Actually Live'), day 0.

## What you're building this week
You have been handling secrets casually this whole track, an AWS key here, a database password there, a Kubernetes Secret that is really just base64. This week you fix that properly. Secrets management is one of the highest-stakes decisions in infrastructure, because how you store, deliver, rotate, and audit a credential determines whether a breach exposes one system or all of them. By Sunday your app gets its real secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, delivered into Kubernetes by the External Secrets Operator, with no password committed anywhere and a path to rotation, the genuine production answer to "where do credentials actually live."

## Why this is a security decision, not a config detail
A secret is any value that grants access: API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys, OAuth client secrets, SSH keys. The reason this is consequential is blast radius. A hardcoded secret in git is exposed to everyone who ever clones the repo, forever, and is copied onto every developer's laptop, one leak and an attacker has a key that never expires. Good secrets management shrinks that blast radius: short-lived credentials, delivered only to the workloads that need them, logged when accessed, and revocable. The difference between casual and careful here is the difference between a contained incident and a full compromise.

## The ladder you are climbing this week
There is a clear hierarchy from worst to best, and the week walks up it. Worst: secrets hardcoded in source. Bad: environment variables set by hand on a server (unrotated, unaudited, visible in the process environment). Better: Kubernetes Secrets (RBAC-gated, but base64, not encrypted at rest by default). Best for most teams: a real secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) as the source of truth, synced into Kubernetes for delivery. Knowing where each option sits on that ladder is what lets you look at any system and say how exposed its credentials are.

## Where this fits
You move your app's secrets from wherever they currently live into AWS Secrets Manager, sync them into the cluster with the External Secrets Operator, and set up rotation. This is the security backbone the CI/CD and GitOps weeks lean on, because automated deploys are only safe if the credentials they handle are managed properly.

days.title: What counts as a secret
days.summary: Focus: What counts as a secret

items.title: What counts as a secret
items.body:
## Wider than you think
The first failure is not knowing what to protect. A secret is anything that grants access or proves identity, and the list is longer than the obvious passwords: database credentials and API keys, yes, but also TLS private keys, OAuth client secrets, SSH private keys, webhook signing secrets, JWT signing keys, and session-encryption keys. A useful test: if leaking this value would let someone do something they should not, or impersonate something they are not, it is a secret. Connection strings hide them (a database URL often contains the password), and so do "config" files that quietly carry a token.

## What is NOT a secret, and why the distinction matters
Equally important is the other direction, because treating everything as a secret is its own failure. Non-secret configuration, the log level, a feature flag, a public API endpoint, the region, a bucket name, belongs in a ConfigMap or a values file, in plain sight, where it is easy to read and change. Mixing the two causes real problems: bury a log-level setting in a secret store and nobody can find it; put a real password in a ConfigMap and you have leaked it. The skill from W9's ConfigMap-vs-Secret lesson generalises here, sort every value into "grants access" (secret) or "just configuration" (not), and store each accordingly.

## The leak paths to design against
Knowing what a secret is only helps if you also know how they escape, because secrets leak through predictable channels. The usual ones: committed to git (and living in history forever, even after you delete the line), printed into application logs, baked into a container image layer, pasted into a chat or a ticket, or sitting in a plaintext environment variable readable by anything on the box. Designing secrets management is largely closing these paths, keep secrets out of source and images, scrub them from logs, and deliver them at runtime from a managed store rather than freezing them into artifacts that travel.

## Where this fits
Audit your own project for every value that grants access, and sort your current configuration into "secret" and "not secret." That inventory is the input to the rest of the week, you cannot put your secrets in a proper store until you have correctly identified which values actually are secrets, and which were just configuration wearing a scary name.

items.title: AWS Secrets Manager + Parameter Store
items.body:
## Your cloud already has a secret store
On AWS you do not need to stand up Vault to do this right, two managed services cover most needs. AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets, encrypts them at rest with KMS, gates access with IAM, logs every read in CloudTrail, and can automatically rotate the big ones (notably RDS passwords). SSM Parameter Store is a lighter, cheaper option: `SecureString` parameters give you KMS-encrypted, IAM-gated values without the rotation features, which is plenty for an API key you just need stored safely.
```bash
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name edge/db \
  --secret-string '{"username":"edge","password":"..."}'
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id edge/db --query SecretString
```

## Why a managed store beats a file or an env var
The point is not just "a place to put passwords," it is the four properties a flat file or an env var cannot give you: encryption at rest (KMS), access control (IAM decides exactly which roles can read which secret), an audit trail (CloudTrail logs every access, so after an incident you can see who read what), and rotation hooks. A secret in Secrets Manager is encrypted, permissioned, and logged; the same secret in a `.env` on a server is none of those. That gap is the entire reason this category of tool exists.

## Which one, and the IAM tie-in
The practical split: Parameter Store `SecureString` for simple static secrets where cost matters (cheaper, and free at the standard tier), Secrets Manager when you want built-in rotation or are storing structured database credentials. Either way, the access control is IAM, which connects straight to W14: your pod, via IRSA, assumes a role allowed to read exactly its own secret and nothing else. So "who can read this secret" is answered by the same IAM model you already set up, no new credential to manage, the pod's role is the permission.

## Where this fits
Move one real secret (your database credentials or an API key) into Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and scope an IAM policy so only your app's role can read it. You now have a proper source of truth for that secret, encrypted and audited, which is exactly what tomorrow's Kubernetes delivery and the External Secrets Operator will pull from.

items.title: Kubernetes Secrets
items.body:
## A delivery mechanism, not a vault
Revisiting W9's Secret with clear eyes. A Kubernetes Secret is how a credential reaches a pod, as an environment variable or a mounted file, and at that job it is fine. What it is not is a secure store. Two limits to hold onto: its values are base64-encoded, which is encoding, not encryption (anyone who can read the Secret reads the value with one command), and it is not encrypted at rest in etcd by default. So a Kubernetes Secret is only as safe as access to your cluster's etcd and your RBAC, and it should never be your system of record for a secret.

## Make the delivery layer as safe as it can be
Given it is the delivery mechanism, you still harden it. Turn on encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd (an EKS cluster can use a KMS key for this, so etcd no longer holds plaintext). Lock down RBAC so only the service accounts that need a given Secret can read it, a Secret readable by every pod in the namespace is a Secret one compromised pod leaks. And keep the Secret's contents out of git: never commit a Secret manifest with a real value, which is the whole reason the next lesson exists. These steps do not make a Kubernetes Secret a vault; they make it a reasonable last hop.

## The git problem this creates
Here is the tension that sets up tomorrow. Everything else in your cluster is declarative YAML you commit to git (that is the GitOps direction of W18). But you cannot commit a Secret with a real password in it, that is the cardinal sin from D2. So how do secrets fit a GitOps world where the repo is the source of truth? The wrong answers are committing them anyway, or hand-creating them with `kubectl` outside of git (now your cluster has state that is not in the repo). The right answer is to keep the real secret in an external store and sync it in, which is exactly what the External Secrets Operator does.

## Where this fits
Enable encryption at rest for your cluster's Secrets and tighten RBAC so each Secret is readable only by its pod's service account. You have made the delivery layer as safe as it gets, and surfaced the real problem, getting secrets into the cluster without committing them, that the External Secrets Operator solves tomorrow.

items.title: External Secrets Operator (ESO)
items.body:
## Bridge the store to the cluster
The External Secrets Operator resolves yesterday's tension cleanly. It is a controller you install in the cluster that watches a new object, an `ExternalSecret`, which is safe to commit because it contains only a reference, not a value. ESO reads that reference, fetches the real secret from AWS Secrets Manager (or Vault, or others), and creates a normal Kubernetes Secret from it for your pods to consume:
```yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: edge-db
spec:
  secretStoreRef: { name: aws-secrets, kind: SecretStore }
  target: { name: edge-db }          # the K8s Secret ESO will create
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef: { key: edge/db, property: password }   # points at AWS, no value here
```
The real password lives only in AWS Secrets Manager; the cluster gets a synced copy; and the YAML in git names a location, not a credential.

## Why this is the answer to the GitOps secret problem
This is the pattern that makes secrets and GitOps compatible. Your whole cluster state, including how secrets are wired, lives in git as `ExternalSecret` manifests that are safe to read, while the actual values stay in the managed store with its encryption, IAM, and audit trail. ESO also keeps the Kubernetes Secret in sync: rotate the value in AWS Secrets Manager and ESO refreshes the cluster copy on its next reconcile, so rotation upstream propagates without you hand-editing anything. You get the cloud store's security and the cluster's convenient delivery, joined by a reference you can safely version-control.

## The trust boundary to keep clear
One thing to reason about: ESO needs permission to read the external store, so it (via IRSA) holds the keys to fetch secrets. That makes the operator and its IAM role a sensitive component, scope its access tightly (it should read only the secrets it must sync) and treat its role as privileged. The win is still large, you replaced "a real password committed in git or hand-created with kubectl" with "a reference in git plus a tightly-scoped operator", but be deliberate about what that operator is allowed to read.

## Where this fits
Install ESO, point it at the secret you put in AWS Secrets Manager yesterday, and let it create the Kubernetes Secret your app consumes. Your secret now lives in one secure place, is delivered to pods automatically, and is wired up entirely through git-safe YAML, the production-grade answer this week was building toward.

items.title: Secret rotation
items.body:
## Static secrets are the ones that get stolen
A password that never changes is a password that, once leaked, works forever. Rotation, changing secrets on a schedule or on demand, shrinks that window: even if a credential leaks, it stops working at the next rotation, so the value of a stolen secret decays. This is why rotation is the property that separates mature secrets management from "we put the passwords in a nicer box." A store that holds static secrets safely is good; one that also rotates them limits the damage of the leak you did not detect.

## Managed rotation, and the dynamic-secret idea
Two levels. Managed rotation: AWS Secrets Manager can rotate supported secrets (notably RDS passwords) on a schedule by running a rotation function that changes the password in both the database and the secret, atomically, so apps reading from the secret pick up the new one with no outage. Dynamic secrets (HashiCorp Vault's signature feature) go further and are worth understanding even if you use AWS day to day: instead of storing a database password at all, the app asks Vault at startup, Vault creates a short-lived database user that expires in an hour, and revokes it after. There is no long-lived password to steal, because the credential barely outlives the request that needed it.

## Why rotation is mostly an architecture problem
The hard part of rotation is rarely the rotating, it is that your application must tolerate the credential changing underneath it. An app that reads a password once at boot and caches it forever breaks the moment the secret rotates. So rotation forces a design property: fetch or refresh credentials such that a change is picked up without a manual restart, which the ESO sync from yesterday helps with, and which dynamic secrets demand outright. This is why teams that "cannot rotate" usually have an application problem, not a secrets-store problem, the store is willing; the app cannot cope.

## Where this fits
Turn on automatic rotation for your database secret in AWS Secrets Manager (or, at minimum, write down the rotation policy and confirm your app re-reads the secret rather than caching it at boot). You have now closed the loop, secrets that live in a secure store, reach pods safely, and change on a schedule so a leak has a short shelf life, the full shape of production secrets management.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app's credentials now live and move like production credentials. By tonight:
- the real secret (database creds or an API key) lives in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypted with KMS, readable only by your app's IAM role.
- the External Secrets Operator syncs it into a Kubernetes Secret from a git-safe `ExternalSecret` manifest, with no value committed anywhere.
- your pod consumes the secret normally, with no password in the image, the repo, or an env var on a box.
- rotation is configured (or its policy written), so the secret's leaked shelf life is short.

## The test that proves it
Run the grep that should come back empty. Search your whole repo and its git history for the real secret value (`git log -p | grep <secret>`), it must not appear, anywhere, ever. Then confirm the live path works end to end: the value exists only in Secrets Manager, ESO created the cluster Secret, and the pod can read it. The combination, "the secret is nowhere in git, yet the running pod has it", is the exact property good secrets management delivers, and being able to demonstrate both halves is the deliverable.

## Ship the artifact
Document the secrets architecture in a `docs/secrets.md`: where secrets live (AWS Secrets Manager), how they reach pods (ESO, with the `ExternalSecret` reference pattern), how access is controlled (IAM via IRSA), and the rotation policy. Include the explicit rule that no real secret value ever goes in the repo. This document is a strong portfolio signal, it shows you understand secrets as a security architecture, not just a place to dump passwords, which is exactly the maturity a reviewer is looking for.

## Where this fits in the track
You have closed the most security-sensitive gap in the stack: credentials are now stored, delivered, and rotated properly, on the cloud you committed to. This is the backbone the automation weeks require, because CI/CD (W17) and GitOps (W18) move deploys, and an automated deploy is only as safe as the secrets it handles. With the platform now built, secured, and defined as code, the rest of the track turns to shipping changes onto it quickly and safely.

weeks.title: CI/CD, From Push to Production in Minutes
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery in the DevOps/Cloud context is different from the application developer's CI/CD. As an infrastructure engineer, you are building the CI/CD systems that other teams use, managing deployments across multiple services and environments, and ensuring the pipeline itself is reliable, secure, and fast.

A mature CI/CD pipeline is not just "run tests and deploy." It is: source code → lint and type check → unit tests → integration tests → build Docker image → scan image for vulnerabilities → push to registry → deploy to staging → run smoke tests → deploy to production → monitor for anomalies → roll back if needed.

The deployment strategies that matter in production. Rolling update: replace pods one at a time, always some old, some new, then all new. Kubernetes Deployments use this by default. Zero downtime but requires both old and new code to serve requests simultaneously (backward-compatible API changes). Blue-green: two identical environments (blue is live, green gets the new version). After green is tested, the load balancer switches all traffic from blue to green. Instant cutover, easy rollback (switch back to blue), but 2x the resource cost. Canary: route a small percentage of traffic to the new version. If error rates are acceptable, gradually increase. Requires sophisticated traffic splitting (Istio, Argo Rollouts).

Argo CD is the GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. You commit desired cluster state to a git repository. Argo CD watches the repository and continuously reconciles the cluster to match git. This separates CI (building and testing code) from CD (deploying to Kubernetes). CI produces an image and commits the new image tag to the gitops repository. Argo CD detects the commit and deploys.

GitHub Actions secrets and OIDC: instead of storing cloud credentials (AWS access keys) as GitHub Secrets, use OIDC. GitHub Actions gets a short-lived token from GitHub's OIDC provider. AWS, GCP, and Azure can be configured to trust this token and exchange it for cloud credentials. No long-lived credentials to manage or rotate.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You have deployed your app to EKS by hand, `helm install` and `kubectl apply`, run when you remember to. This week a `git push` does it for you. You build a real CI/CD pipeline: code is linted, type-checked, and tested; a Docker image is built and scanned for vulnerabilities; the image is pushed to a registry; and the app deploys, first to staging, then to production. By Sunday, merging a pull request is the entire deploy process, and you understand the deployment strategies (rolling, blue-green, canary) that let that happen without taking the site down.

## Why an infrastructure engineer thinks about CI/CD differently
As an app developer, CI/CD is "my tests run and my code deploys." As the infrastructure engineer, you are building the pipeline other teams use, and that shifts what matters. The pipeline itself must be reliable (a flaky pipeline blocks everyone), secure (it holds the keys to production), and fast (a slow pipeline is a tax on every change). You are not just automating your deploy; you are building the paved road that makes everyone's deploys safe and boring, which is a different and more valuable skill than scripting one deploy.

## The shape of a mature pipeline
A real pipeline is more than "test and deploy." The full chain is: source, lint and type-check, unit tests, integration tests, build image, scan image, push to registry, deploy to staging, smoke test, deploy to production, watch for anomalies, roll back if needed. Each stage is a gate: failure stops the line before a bad change reaches users. You will not build every stage to perfection this week, but you will build the spine of it and understand why each gate exists, because a pipeline missing the scan or the staging step is exactly where bad deploys slip through.

## Where this fits
You wire up CI/CD for your Edge Portfolio so a merge builds, scans, and deploys it to EKS automatically. This is also the setup for next week: CI's job ends at "a new image exists," and W18's GitOps picks up from there to deploy it, the clean split between building code and reconciling the cluster.

items.title: CI vs CD vs CD
items.body:
## Three letters, three jobs
The acronym hides that "CI/CD" is really three distinct things, and the famous ambiguity is the two CDs:
- **CI (Continuous Integration):** every push is automatically built and tested, so integration problems surface in minutes, not at a big scary merge. The point is that the main branch is always in a known-good, tested state.
- **CD (Continuous Delivery):** every change that passes CI is automatically prepared and made deployable, a release is one button-press away, but a human decides when to push it.
- **CD (Continuous Deployment):** the stronger version, every change that passes CI is deployed to production automatically, no human gate at all.

## Delivery vs deployment is a real decision, not pedantry
The difference between the two CDs is a genuine choice about how much you trust your pipeline. Continuous Deployment (auto to prod) demands a mature pipeline: comprehensive tests, automated rollback, good monitoring, because there is no human to catch a bad change before users do. Continuous Delivery keeps a human approval before prod, which is the right call when your tests do not yet cover enough, or when a regulator or a customer contract requires a person to sign off. Most teams start at Continuous Delivery and earn their way to Continuous Deployment as their tests and monitoring get good enough to trust. Knowing which one you are doing, and why, is the actual literacy here.

## What gates the pipeline
Across all three, the pipeline is a sequence of gates, and a failure at any gate stops the line. Tests failing stops the merge. A vulnerability scan over threshold stops the build. A failed smoke test in staging stops the promotion to prod. This is the whole value proposition: the pipeline mechanically prevents an unverified change from advancing, so "it passed CI" actually means something. A pipeline with no real gates is just an expensive way to deploy bugs faster.

## Where this fits
Decide, for your Edge Portfolio, whether you are doing Continuous Delivery (with an approval before prod) or Continuous Deployment (fully automatic), and why. That choice shapes the pipeline you build this week, specifically whether D6's manual approval gate exists, and it is the framing every later day builds on.

items.title: GitLab CI
items.body:
## A second CI system, to see what is universal
You will mostly use GitHub Actions on this track, but spending a day on GitLab CI is worth it, because seeing two systems teaches you which concepts are universal and which are just one tool's syntax. The shared shape is the same everywhere: a pipeline is a set of jobs grouped into ordered stages, jobs in a stage run in parallel, stages run in sequence, and each job runs on a runner in a defined environment. Learn that mental model and you can read any CI system's config, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jenkins, after a short adjustment.

## What GitLab CI looks like
GitLab CI is configured in a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the repo root:
```yaml
stages: [test, build, deploy]

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script: npm ci && npm test

build-image:
  stage: build
  script: docker build -t $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  environment: staging
  script: helm upgrade --install edge ./chart -f values-staging.yaml
```
Map this onto GitHub Actions and the correspondence is direct: stages and jobs are the same idea, `script` is `run`, `$CI_COMMIT_SHA` is `${{ github.sha }}`. The differences are surface; the structure is identical.

## Why the comparison matters in practice
This is not trivia, it is portability of your own skill. Companies run different CI systems, and the one with the loudest fans is not always the one you will inherit. An engineer who understands "stages, jobs, runners, artifacts, environments" can be productive on whichever system the job uses, while one who only memorised GitHub Actions YAML has to relearn from scratch. GitLab CI also bundles the registry, the repo, and the runner in one product, a useful contrast with GitHub's more pick-and-choose model, and a reason some companies pick it.

## Where this fits
Write a small `.gitlab-ci.yml` (even if you do not run it) that mirrors the pipeline you are building in GitHub Actions, and notice how little actually changes. You are inoculating yourself against tool lock-in at the skill level: the pipeline you can build is a concept, not a vendor's YAML dialect.

items.title: Build-once, deploy-many
items.body:
## The principle that prevents "works in staging, breaks in prod"
A foundational pipeline rule, simple to state and easy to violate: build your artifact exactly once, then deploy that same artifact to every environment. The image you tested in staging is the byte-for-byte image you promote to production, identified by an immutable tag (the git SHA, not `latest`). The anti-pattern is rebuilding per environment, a `docker build` for staging, another for prod, because the second build can differ (a dependency moved, a base image updated) and now "passed in staging" guarantees nothing about prod. Build once, and what you tested is what you ship.

## What "deploy-many" means concretely
The same immutable image flows through environments, and only the configuration changes per environment, exactly the Helm values-file pattern from W11:
```text
CI builds edge:9f3a1c  (once)
  -> deploy edge:9f3a1c to staging with values-staging.yaml
  -> (tests pass)
  -> deploy edge:9f3a1c to prod    with values-prod.yaml
```
The image tag is the same `9f3a1c` everywhere; staging and prod differ only in replica counts, resource limits, and which secrets they point at. This is why W11's per-environment values files mattered: they are the seam that lets one tested image serve many environments without a rebuild.

## Why immutable tags are non-negotiable
Tag images by the git SHA (or a semver release), never deploy `latest`. `latest` is a moving target: two deploys of "latest" can run different code, rollbacks become ambiguous (roll back to which `latest`?), and you lose the exact-version traceability that lets you say "prod is running commit 9f3a1c." An immutable tag makes every deploy reproducible and every rollback precise. This is the same reproducibility principle as pinning Helm and Terraform versions, applied to the image itself: the artifact you point at must mean exactly one thing, forever.

## Where this fits
Make your pipeline build the image once, tagged by SHA, and deploy that identical tag to staging and then prod with different values files. You have eliminated a whole class of "but it worked in staging" failures, and set up the clean handoff to GitOps next week, where CI's only job is to produce that one immutable image and record its tag.

items.title: Canary and blue-green deploys at the K8s level (Argo Rollouts, Flagger)
items.body:
## Three ways to replace running code without an outage
Deploying a new version to live traffic is the risky moment, and there are three established strategies, each a different tradeoff between safety, cost, and complexity:
- **Rolling update** (Kubernetes' default, from W9): replace pods a few at a time, old and new serve simultaneously until all are new. Zero downtime, no extra cost, but it requires the new and old versions to be compatible (a breaking API or schema change mid-roll will hurt).
- **Blue-green:** run two full environments, blue (live) and green (new). Test green, then switch all traffic at once. Instant cutover and instant rollback (switch back to blue), at the cost of running two copies (2x resources) during the switch.
- **Canary:** send a small slice of traffic (5%) to the new version, watch its error rate, ramp up if healthy, roll back if not. The safest for risky changes, and the most complex, because it needs real traffic-splitting and metric analysis.

## The tools that automate canary
Doing canary by hand (shift weights, watch dashboards, decide) is tedious and error-prone, so two tools automate the loop on top of Kubernetes. Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment with a `Rollout` resource that has canary and blue-green strategies built in, with steps like "10% for 5 minutes, then 50%, then 100%." Flagger drives the same progressive rollout using a service mesh or ingress for traffic-splitting (connecting back to W12) and automatically promotes or rolls back based on metrics (request success rate, latency) it queries from Prometheus. Both turn "watch the canary and decide" into a policy the system executes for you.

## Choosing the strategy for the change
The honest rule is to match the strategy to the risk, not to always reach for the fanciest one. A small, backward-compatible change is fine with a rolling update, do not over-engineer it. Reach for blue-green when you need an instant, clean cutover and can afford the double resources (a risky release where you want a one-click rollback). Reach for canary when the change is genuinely risky and you want real users to validate it in small numbers before everyone sees it (a new checkout flow, a model change). Most deploys are rolling updates; canary and blue-green are tools you bring out for the changes that warrant the extra care.

## Where this fits
Set up a canary or blue-green rollout for your app with Argo Rollouts (or Flagger), deploy a deliberately-broken version, and watch it get caught and rolled back before it reaches all users. Seeing the system refuse to fully promote a bad release is the point, it is the safety net that makes frequent deploys feel safe instead of terrifying.

items.title: Approvals + manual gates
items.body:
## Where a human still belongs in an automated pipeline
A fully automated pipeline is the goal, and there are still places a human pause is the right call, the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment from D2. A manual approval gate gives a named person a moment to say "yes, ship this to prod" before the deploy proceeds. The skill is using gates deliberately, not reflexively: too many and your pipeline is just a slow manual process with extra steps; too few and a risky change reaches prod with nobody having looked. The gate is for the moments where human judgement genuinely adds safety the tests cannot.

## When a gate earns its place
Good reasons for a manual gate, all real:
- **Production deploys you are not yet confident automating**, when your tests and monitoring do not yet cover enough to trust a fully automatic prod deploy.
- **Compliance and change control**, a regulator or customer contract requires a named human to authorise a production change.
- **High-blast-radius changes**, a database migration, a change to the payment path, where the cost of being wrong justifies a deliberate pause.
Bad reasons (gates as a crutch): gating every routine change because the pipeline is not trusted, which just trains everyone to click "approve" without looking, the worst of both worlds.

## How approval gates actually work
In GitHub Actions this is an environment protection rule: the `production` environment requires a reviewer's approval, so the deploy job pauses and waits for a named person (or team) to approve in the UI before it runs. The approval is recorded, who approved, when, giving you an audit trail of every production change. The mechanism is simple; the discipline is in scoping it. A common mature pattern: staging deploys are fully automatic (fast feedback), and only the staging-to-prod promotion has the gate, so you get speed where it is safe and a deliberate human check only at the last, highest-stakes step.

## Where this fits
Add a manual approval gate on your pipeline's production deploy (a GitHub environment protection rule), while leaving staging fully automatic. You have now built the realistic shape most teams actually run, automated up to prod, with one deliberate human check at the riskiest moment, and you can articulate exactly why that gate is there and what it would take to remove it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A `git push` now deploys your app. By tonight, merging a pull request triggers a pipeline that:
- lints, type-checks, and tests the code, stopping the line on any failure.
- builds the Docker image once, tagged by git SHA, and scans it (the Trivy step from W7) before pushing it.
- deploys that exact image to staging automatically, then to production behind a manual approval gate.
- uses OIDC for cloud access, so there are no long-lived AWS keys stored as GitHub Secrets.

## The OIDC detail worth calling out
One security upgrade this week bakes in: your pipeline authenticates to AWS with OIDC, not stored access keys. GitHub Actions requests a short-lived token from GitHub's OIDC provider; AWS is configured to trust that token and exchange it for temporary credentials. The payoff is that there is no AWS access key sitting in your GitHub Secrets to leak or rotate, the same "no long-lived credential" principle as W14's IRSA, now applied to your CI system. A pipeline that holds permanent prod keys is a breach waiting to happen; one that mints short-lived tokens per run is not.

## The test that proves it
Make a trivial visible change (edit a line of the portfolio), open a PR, merge it, and watch the whole chain run untouched: tests pass, image builds and scans, staging deploys, you approve, prod deploys, and your change is live, with you having typed no deploy command. Then make a change that breaks a test and watch the pipeline refuse to advance it. The pair, a good change flowing to prod hands-free and a bad change stopped cold, is the entire deliverable: deployment is now a property of merging, gated by checks that actually mean something.

## Where this fits in the track
You have automated the path from code to production, with the gates (tests, scan, approval) that make automation safe rather than reckless. But notice the seam this week deliberately left: CI's job ends at "a new, tested image exists and its tag is recorded." Next week, GitOps (Argo CD) takes over the deploy half, the cluster continuously reconciles itself to what git says, which is a cleaner and more auditable way to do the deploy part than a pipeline running `helm upgrade`. You built the push-to-prod pipeline; now you make the cluster pull its own desired state.

The CD step: commit the new image tag to the gitops repository (update image: ghcr.io/org/app:NEWSHA in the Kubernetes deployment manifest). Argo CD compares the desired state (new image tag) to actual cluster state (old image tag) and applies the change, rolling update in Kubernetes. Argo CD monitors the rollout status and reports success or failure.

weeks.title: GitOps, Argo CD and Declarative Deploys
weeks.context:
GitOps is the operational model where the desired state of your infrastructure and applications is stored in git, and automation continuously reconciles actual state to match the desired state. The git repository becomes the single source of truth: if it is in git, it is deployed; if it is not in git, it should not exist. The phrase "GitOps" was coined by Weaveworks in 2017; the pattern is now widely adopted.

The two principles of GitOps: declarative (the desired state is expressed declaratively, what you want, not how to get there) and continuous reconciliation (an operator continuously watches git and applies any diff to the live system, not just on deploy commands). Argo CD and Flux are the two dominant GitOps operators for Kubernetes.

Flux CD is the CNCF-graduated alternative to Argo CD. Flux is more GitOps-pure (all configuration is Kubernetes Custom Resources) and more modular. Its components: source-controller (watches git, Helm, and OCI registries), kustomize-controller (applies kustomizations), helm-controller (reconciles HelmReleases), notification-controller (sends alerts), image-automation-controller (updates image tags automatically when a new image is pushed to a registry). Together, these form a fully automated deployment pipeline with no manual steps.

Image automation with Flux: when your CI pushes a new Docker image (myapp:SHA) to a registry, Flux's image-automation-controller detects the new tag (based on your tag policy, latest, semver, or regex), commits a change to your gitops repository updating the image tag, and then the reconciliation loop deploys the new image. This closes the loop: push code → CI builds image → Flux detects new image → Flux updates git → Flux deploys. No human involvement after the PR merge.

Multi-tenancy in Argo CD / Flux: multiple teams sharing a cluster, each managing their own namespace. Argo CD has Projects that define which git repos and namespaces a team can deploy to. Flux has Tenants and NS-level Kustomizations. The infrastructure team manages the cluster itself (cluster controllers, monitoring, networking); application teams manage their applications in their assigned namespaces.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Last week's pipeline ended with `helm upgrade` pushing to the cluster, the pipeline reaching INTO production to deploy. This week you invert that. With GitOps, you commit your desired cluster state to a git repository, and an operator running inside the cluster (Argo CD) continuously watches that repo and makes the cluster match it. Nobody pushes to the cluster anymore; the cluster pulls its own truth from git. By Sunday your Edge Portfolio deploys by a commit to a git repo, Argo CD notices and reconciles, and the live cluster is, by construction, exactly what git says it should be.

## Why "pull from git" beats "push to cluster"
The shift from a pipeline pushing deploys to a cluster pulling its state sounds subtle and changes a lot. Git becomes the single source of truth: if it is in git it is deployed, if it is not in git it should not exist, and the live state of the cluster is auditable by reading a repo. You get a complete history (every change is a commit, with an author, a diff, and a revert), and your CI system no longer needs powerful credentials to push into prod, the operator inside the cluster pulls, so the keys to production never leave the cluster. Deploys become reviewable pull requests instead of imperative commands run from someone's laptop or a CI job.

## The mental model: desired state, one more time
You already know this model; GitOps just moves it up a level. Kubernetes reconciles pods toward the desired state in its API. GitOps reconciles the entire cluster's API toward the desired state in git. It is the same controller-and-reconciliation idea from W9, now with git as the source of truth and Argo CD as the controller closing the gap. Once that clicks, GitOps stops being a buzzword and becomes the obvious extension: if declarative desired state is good for pods, it is good for everything, and git is where declarative state belongs.

## Where this fits
You put your app's manifests and Helm config in a git repo, install Argo CD, and let it deploy and continuously reconcile your app on EKS. This is the deploy half that W17's CI handed off to: CI produces an image and records its tag in git, Argo CD sees the change and deploys, the full loop with no human pushing to the cluster.

items.title: GitOps principles
items.body:
## Two ideas do all the work
GitOps rests on two principles, and everything else follows from them:
- **Declarative:** the desired state is expressed as what you want (a Deployment with 3 replicas of this image), not a script of how to get there. Your whole system is described by data in git, not by imperative commands.
- **Continuous reconciliation:** an operator continuously compares the live cluster to git and applies any difference, not only when you run a deploy, but always. If the cluster drifts from git, the operator pulls it back.

## Why continuous reconciliation is the real upgrade
The continuous part is what separates GitOps from "we keep our YAML in git and run `kubectl apply` in CI." Plenty of teams store manifests in git and apply them in a pipeline; that is version-controlled deploys, not GitOps. The difference is that a GitOps operator is always watching and always correcting. If someone runs a manual `kubectl edit` on the cluster at 2am, a pipeline would never know, but the operator notices the cluster no longer matches git and reverts it. Git is not just where you keep the YAML; it is the live, enforced source of truth, and the cluster is continuously dragged back toward it.

## What the model gives you, concretely
The two principles together buy real properties. Auditability: the deployed state is a git repo, so "what is running in prod" is a question you answer by reading a file, and "what changed and who changed it" is `git log`. Easy rollback: reverting a deploy is `git revert`, the operator reconciles back to the previous state. Security: the operator pulls from git, so your CI system and developers never need credentials to write to the cluster directly. Consistency: stand up a new cluster, point the operator at the same repo, and you get an identical environment. These are not separate features; they all fall out of "git is the source of truth and an operator enforces it."

## Where this fits
Hold these two principles as the test for everything you set up this week: is the desired state declarative and in git, and is something continuously reconciling the cluster to it? Argo CD (and Flux) are just implementations of this idea, and judging any deployment setup by these two principles tells you immediately whether it is real GitOps or just YAML-in-git with extra steps.

items.title: Flux
items.body:
## The other GitOps operator
Argo CD is the one you are using this week; Flux is the other dominant GitOps operator, CNCF-graduated, and worth understanding because you will meet both. Where Argo CD ships with a polished web UI and an app-centric model, Flux is more GitOps-pure and modular: everything is configured as Kubernetes custom resources (there is no separate UI that is the source of truth, the cluster's own API is), and it is built from focused controllers you compose. The two solve the same problem with different philosophies, Argo CD leans toward an opinionated product with a dashboard, Flux toward a toolkit of Kubernetes-native pieces.

## Flux's controllers, and why the breakdown matters
Flux is a set of cooperating controllers, and the names tell you what GitOps needs: source-controller watches git, Helm, and OCI registries for the desired state; kustomize-controller applies Kustomize overlays; helm-controller reconciles `HelmRelease` objects; notification-controller sends alerts; and image-automation-controller updates image tags automatically. Seeing GitOps decomposed this way is clarifying even if you run Argo CD, it shows the moving parts any GitOps system must have: something to watch sources, something to apply config, something to notify, something to bump images.

## Image automation, the loop-closer
Flux's standout feature is image automation, worth understanding as the thing that fully closes the deploy loop. When your CI pushes a new image (`edge:9f3a1c`) to the registry, the image-automation-controller detects the new tag (by your policy, semver or regex), commits a change to your GitOps repo bumping the image tag, and the normal reconciliation then deploys it. The full loop becomes: push code, CI builds and pushes the image, Flux detects the image, Flux updates git, Flux deploys, with no human after the PR merge. Argo CD typically pairs with a separate tool (Argo CD Image Updater) for this; Flux builds it in. Either way, this is the seam where W17's "CI produces an image" connects to "the cluster deploys it."

## Where this fits
Read how Flux's controllers and image automation work, and map them onto the Argo CD setup you are building, the two are different packagings of the same GitOps ideas. Knowing both means you can walk into a team running either and understand what you are looking at, and you can reason about the one feature (automatic image updates) that fully removes humans from the deploy path.

items.title: Auto-sync vs manual sync
items.body:
## Who pulls the trigger on a detected change
Argo CD notices when git and the cluster differ; the question this day answers is what it does next. In manual sync, Argo CD shows the diff and waits, a human clicks "Sync" to apply it. In auto-sync, Argo CD applies the change automatically as soon as it appears in git, no click. This is the GitOps version of W17's Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment distinction: manual sync keeps a human between git and the cluster, auto-sync removes them, and the choice depends on how much you trust the path.

## The tradeoff, environment by environment
The right answer is usually different per environment, and the pattern most teams land on is sensible: auto-sync in dev and staging (you want fast, hands-free feedback there, and a mistake is cheap), manual sync, or auto-sync with care, in production (a deliberate human apply, or strong guardrails, at the highest-stakes step). Auto-sync also pairs with two sub-options worth knowing: prune (delete cluster resources that were removed from git, powerful and a little scary, since it makes git deletions real deletions) and self-heal (revert any manual change to the cluster immediately, the strongest form of "git is truth"). Turning those on means the cluster is fully subordinate to git; leaving them off keeps a softer hand.

## Why this is a trust dial, not a setting
Think of auto-sync, prune, and self-heal as one dial for "how literally is git the truth." All the way up (auto-sync plus prune plus self-heal) means the cluster is exactly git, always, instantly, no manual change survives, no orphaned resource lingers, which is beautiful when your git workflow is solid and dangerous when it is not (a bad merge deploys instantly, a wrong deletion prunes prod). All the way down (manual sync) means git is a strong suggestion a human confirms. Mature teams turn the dial up as their review and testing discipline earns it, exactly mirroring the journey from Continuous Delivery to Continuous Deployment.

## Where this fits
Configure auto-sync for your staging environment and manual sync (or auto-sync without prune) for production, and decide consciously whether to enable self-heal. You are tuning how strictly your cluster obeys git, which is the central operational decision in running GitOps, and you can now explain the tradeoff rather than just flipping a switch.
