items.title: Drift detection
items.body:
## When the cluster stops matching git
Drift is any difference between what git says and what is actually running, and it is the condition GitOps exists to catch. It happens constantly in the real world: someone runs `kubectl edit` to hotfix an incident at 3am, an autoscaler or another controller changes a field, a half-finished manual experiment is left behind. In a non-GitOps world this drift is invisible, the cluster quietly diverges from any record of what it should be, until the next deploy stomps the manual fix or, worse, silently depends on it. GitOps makes drift visible and, if you let it, self-correcting.

## What Argo CD does about it
Argo CD continuously compares live state to git and reports each application's sync status: `Synced` (cluster matches git) or `OutOfSync` (drift detected), with a diff showing exactly what differs. From there your sync policy decides the response. With self-heal on, Argo CD reverts the drift automatically, the manual `kubectl edit` is undone within seconds, because git is the truth and the cluster is not allowed to disagree. With self-heal off, Argo CD just flags the drift and shows you the diff, leaving a human to reconcile. Either way, the key win is that drift is now surfaced, not silent.

## The cultural change drift detection forces
Drift detection quietly changes how a team operates, and that is the real point. Once the cluster self-heals to git, the manual `kubectl edit` stops working as a way to change production, your edit gets reverted, so the only durable way to change the cluster is to change git. That feels restrictive at first and is exactly the discipline you want: every production change becomes a reviewable, recorded commit, and "what is running" can never silently diverge from "what we agreed to run." The incident hotfix still happens, it just happens as a fast commit to git, not an untracked edit someone forgets to write down. GitOps does not just detect drift; it removes the incentive to create it.

## Where this fits
Make a manual change to your cluster (`kubectl edit` your Deployment's replica count) and watch Argo CD flag it as OutOfSync, then, with self-heal on, watch it revert your change. Seeing the cluster refuse to drift from git is the GitOps guarantee made concrete, the cluster is not just deployed from git once, it is held equal to git continuously.

items.title: Combining Helm + Kustomize with Argo CD
items.body:
## Argo CD does not replace your packaging tools
You spent W11 on Helm and met Kustomize; this day answers how they fit under GitOps. Argo CD does not make you rewrite your manifests, it renders them. An Argo CD Application points at a path in a git repo and tells Argo CD how to turn it into Kubernetes objects: it can run `helm template` on a Helm chart, build a Kustomize overlay, or apply plain YAML. So your Helm chart from W11 and any Kustomize overlays keep doing exactly what they did; Argo CD becomes the thing that renders and applies them continuously, instead of you running `helm upgrade` by hand.

## The common, powerful combination
The pattern many teams settle on uses both tools together, each for what it is best at, which connects straight back to W11's D6. Use Helm to package the app (the templated chart with all its parameters), and use Kustomize to apply small, environment-specific patches on top of the rendered chart, without forking it. Argo CD supports this directly: render the Helm chart, then run Kustomize over the output to patch the few fields that differ in this environment. You get Helm's packaging and the registry ecosystem, plus Kustomize's readable, template-free per-environment patches, with Argo CD reconciling the final result to the cluster.

## Why this matters: nothing you built is wasted
The reassuring through-line: GitOps is a deployment model, not a replacement for everything underneath it. Your Helm chart, your values files, your Kustomize overlays, your images, all of it still applies, and Argo CD sits on top as the reconciler. This is why the track built up Helm and Kustomize before GitOps: GitOps is the orchestration layer that decides "the cluster should match this rendered config in git," and Helm and Kustomize are still how that config gets produced. Understanding the separation, packaging tools render, the GitOps operator reconciles, keeps you from thinking GitOps is yet another tool that obsoletes the last one.

## Where this fits
Create an Argo CD Application that deploys your Edge Portfolio from your Helm chart in git, optionally with a Kustomize patch for the prod environment, and watch it reconcile. You have now connected everything: the chart from W11, the environments from W13, the secrets from W16, all deployed and continuously reconciled from git, which is the full, production-shaped delivery setup this phase was building toward.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app now deploys by a commit, and the cluster keeps itself honest. By tonight:
- your Edge Portfolio's desired state (Helm chart, values, the image tag) lives in a git repo that is the single source of truth.
- Argo CD runs in the cluster, watches that repo, and reconciles the live app to match it.
- a change is a pull request: merge it, Argo CD notices and deploys; revert it, Argo CD rolls back.
- drift is caught, a manual change to the cluster is flagged (and, with self-heal, reverted) because the cluster is not allowed to disagree with git.

## The test that proves it
Two demonstrations, both fast. First, deploy-by-commit: change the image tag (or a replica count) in the git repo, merge, and watch Argo CD detect the diff and reconcile the cluster, with you having run no `kubectl` or `helm` command. Second, the GitOps guarantee: `kubectl edit` the live Deployment to change something, and watch Argo CD flag it OutOfSync and (with self-heal) revert it. The pair, the cluster following git automatically and refusing to drift from it, is the whole deliverable, and it is a genuinely different and safer operational model than the push-based deploy you started the phase with.

## Ship the artifact

This is a strong portfolio artifact precisely because it demonstrates the operational maturity hiring managers look for in infrastructure roles, you are not just deploying, you are running a declarative, auditable, self-healing delivery system.

## Where this fits in the track
The build-and-ship arc is complete: your app is containerised, packaged, running on a managed cloud cluster defined as code, with secrets handled properly, deployed by an automated pipeline, and continuously reconciled from git. The rest of the track turns from building and shipping to operating, can you tell when it is broken and why (W19 observability), can you set and defend reliability targets (W20 SRE), can you control what it costs (W21), and can you recover when it fails (W22). weeks.title: Observability, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry
weeks.context:
Observability is the ability to understand the internal state of your system from its external outputs. The three pillars: metrics (numeric measurements over time), logs (timestamped event records), and traces (end-to-end request journeys across services). In a containerised, microservices environment, these three together tell the complete story of what your system is doing and why.

Prometheus is the standard metrics system for Kubernetes. It pulls metrics from targets (your applications and Kubernetes components expose metrics at /metrics in the OpenMetrics format). Prometheus stores time-series data: each metric is a time-series of (timestamp, value) pairs with labels. You query metrics with PromQL, a functional query language. Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus and routes them to Slack, PagerDuty, or email based on configurable rules.

Grafana is the visualisation layer. It connects to Prometheus (and many other data sources) and renders dashboards. The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart installs Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, and a set of pre-built dashboards for Kubernetes monitoring in one command. This is the standard starting point for Kubernetes observability.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the standard instrumentation framework. It replaces vendor-specific SDKs (DataDog agent, New Relic agent) with one set of APIs that can export to any backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog). You instrument your application once with the OTel SDK; you can switch observability backends without changing application code. OTel collectors (agents or sidecars) receive telemetry from applications and route it to backends.

Distributed tracing: a single user request in a microservices system may touch 10 services. A trace records the entire journey: each service creates a span (a unit of work with a start time, duration, and metadata). Spans are linked by a trace ID. Viewing the trace shows a waterfall of all spans, which service was slow, where the error occurred, how long each operation took. Jaeger (open source) or Tempo (part of the Grafana stack) store and visualise traces.

PromQL is the query language you must learn to use Prometheus effectively. Key concepts: instant vector (current value), range vector (values over a time range), rate(http_requests_total[5m]) (per-second rate of increase), sum by (status_code) (aggregate by label), histogram_quantile(0.95, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) (95th percentile latency).

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Your app runs on EKS, deployed by GitOps. The obvious next question, and the one this week answers, is: when it breaks at 3am, how do you know, and how do you find out why? Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs, and you build it this week. By Sunday your Edge Portfolio exposes metrics that Prometheus scrapes, you have Grafana dashboards showing its real behaviour, you can follow a single request as a distributed trace, and you understand the three pillars (metrics, logs, traces) well enough to know which one to reach for when something is wrong.

## Why "it's running" was never enough
You have leaned on `kubectl get pods` saying `Running`, and W10 already taught you that "Running" is not "healthy." Observability is the grown-up version of that lesson. A green deploy tells you the process started; it tells you nothing about whether requests are slow, whether the error rate just tripled, or which of ten services is the actual culprit when the page is slow. Production systems fail in ways that do not show up as a crashed pod, and observability is how you see those failures, and crucially, how you diagnose them, instead of guessing and restarting things.

## The three pillars, and the one rule for using them
Metrics, logs, and traces each answer a different question, and knowing which is which is half the skill:
- **Metrics** (numbers over time) answer "is something wrong, and how wrong?", fast to query, cheap to store, good for dashboards and alerts.
- **Logs** (timestamped events) answer "what exactly happened?", the detail for a specific incident.
- **Traces** (a request's journey across services) answer "where, across all my services, did this slow request spend its time?"
The workflow they enable: a metric or alert tells you something is wrong, a trace tells you where, and logs tell you exactly what. Learn to move between them in that order and debugging a distributed system stops being archaeology.

## Where this fits
You instrument your app and stand up the Prometheus/Grafana/Tempo stack on your cluster this week. This is the foundation for everything operational that follows: W20's SLOs are defined in terms of the metrics you collect here, and you cannot set a reliability target you cannot measure.

days.title: Metrics vs logs vs traces

items.title: Metrics vs logs vs traces
items.body:
## Three signals, three jobs
The three pillars are not redundant; each is the right tool for a different question, and reaching for the wrong one is why debugging drags.
- **Metrics** are numeric measurements over time (requests per second, error rate, p99 latency, memory usage). Cheap to store and fast to query, so they power dashboards and alerts. They tell you that something changed, and by how much, but not the specifics of any one request.
- **Logs** are timestamped event records, often with detail (this request, this user, this error message and stack trace). They tell you exactly what happened for a specific event, at the cost of being voluminous and expensive to search.
- **Traces** follow one request across every service it touches, breaking it into spans. They tell you where, in a multi-service path, the time went or the error occurred.

## The debugging path they form together
The pillars are most powerful in sequence, and the sequence is the actual skill. A typical incident: an alert fires off a metric (error rate crossed 1%), so you know there is a problem and roughly its size. You open a trace of a failing request and see it across your services, the checkout service's call to the payment service is the span that errored. You pull the logs for that service at that timestamp and read the exact exception. Metric to trace to logs, from "something is wrong" to "where" to "exactly what", is how you debug a distributed system without grepping ten services by hand.

## Why you need all three, not a favourite
Teams that lean on only one pillar feel the gap. Metrics-only: you know latency spiked but cannot see which request or why. Logs-only: you can read what happened but cannot get a fast "is the whole system healthy" view, and searching logs across services for one request is painful. Traces-only: you see request paths but lack the aggregate trends and the line-level detail. The pillars are complementary by design, and a mature setup wires them together (a trace links to its logs, a dashboard links to traces) so you can move between them in one investigation rather than juggling three disconnected tools.

## Where this fits
Map each pillar to a question you would actually ask about your Edge Portfolio ("is the error rate up?" is a metric, "what did this failed request do?" is a trace and its logs). The rest of the week builds the tooling, Prometheus for metrics, Tempo for traces, your logs alongside, and the value only lands if you know which signal answers which question.

items.title: Grafana
items.body:
## Prometheus collects, Grafana shows
Two tools, one job split. Prometheus is the metrics engine: it periodically scrapes a `/metrics` endpoint on your app and Kubernetes components, stores each metric as a time-series of (timestamp, value) pairs tagged with labels, and answers queries in PromQL. Grafana is the visualisation layer on top: it queries Prometheus (and other sources) and renders dashboards. The standard way to get both on Kubernetes is one Helm chart, `kube-prometheus-stack`, which installs Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, and pre-built Kubernetes dashboards in a single command, the normal starting point for cluster observability.

## The Prometheus model: pull, not push
The thing that surprises people coming from other monitoring tools: Prometheus pulls. It does not wait for your app to send metrics; it scrapes your app's `/metrics` endpoint on a schedule. Your app's job is just to expose current values there (a counter of requests, a histogram of latencies) in the OpenMetrics text format, usually via a small client library. The pull model is why Prometheus fits Kubernetes so well, it discovers pods to scrape automatically as they come and go, with no per-pod configuration to push metrics outward.

## PromQL, the part you must actually learn
Prometheus is only as useful as your ability to query it, and PromQL is worth real practice. A few patterns cover most of what you need:
```promql
rate(http_requests_total[5m])                  # per-second request rate over 5m
sum by (status_code) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))   # rate split by status code
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))      # p95 latency
```
The mental shift is that PromQL works on time-series, not single numbers: `rate(...[5m])` turns an ever-increasing counter into a per-second rate (the form you almost always want), `sum by (label)` aggregates across pods while keeping a dimension you care about, and `histogram_quantile` extracts a percentile from a histogram. These three shapes, a rate, an aggregation, and a quantile, are most of practical PromQL.

## Where this fits
Install `kube-prometheus-stack`, confirm Prometheus is scraping your app's `/metrics`, and build a Grafana panel for your request rate and p95 latency with PromQL. You now have eyes on your app's real behaviour, and the exact metrics (availability, latency) that W20 turns into formal reliability targets.

items.title: Tempo
items.body:
## Seeing a request cross your whole system
Metrics and logs treat each service in isolation; a trace stitches one request's path across all of them. The mechanics: as a request flows through your services, each service records a span, a unit of work with a start time, a duration, and metadata (which operation, success or error). All the spans for one request share a trace ID, so the tracing system can assemble them into a single waterfall: this request spent 12ms in the API, then 340ms waiting on the database, then errored in the payment call. That waterfall is the answer to "the page is slow, but which part is slow," which metrics alone cannot give you.

## Tempo, and where it fits in the Grafana stack
Tempo is Grafana's tracing backend (Jaeger is the other common open-source option), and it is built to be cheap: it stores traces in object storage (S3) and is designed for high volume at low cost. In the Grafana stack it slots in next to Prometheus and your logs, so one Grafana instance shows metrics, traces, and logs together. The payoff of that integration is the workflow from D2 made real: a dashboard panel can link from a latency spike straight to an example trace, and a span in that trace can link to its logs, so you move metric to trace to logs without leaving the tool.

## Why tracing earns its keep in microservices
On a single service, a trace is mildly useful; across ten services, it is the difference between diagnosing in minutes and diagnosing in hours. When a request touches the API, the auth service, the database, and three downstream calls, "it's slow" has ten possible causes, and only a trace shows which span actually consumed the time or threw the error. This is exactly the problem W12's service mesh hinted at and why distributed systems are hard to debug without it: the failure is rarely in the service you are looking at, and the trace points you at the one that matters instead of you guessing across all of them.

## Where this fits
Instrument your app to emit spans (you will do the instrumentation properly with OpenTelemetry tomorrow), send them to Tempo, and view a request's waterfall in Grafana. Seeing one request's journey across services is the third pillar in place, and it completes the metric-to-trace-to-logs debugging path you will rely on for every future incident.

items.title: OpenTelemetry
items.body:
## One instrumentation, any backend
There is a trap in observability: instrument your app with a vendor's SDK (the Datadog agent, the New Relic agent) and your telemetry code is now welded to that vendor, switching means re-instrumenting everything. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the open standard that fixes this. You instrument your application once with the OTel SDK, emitting metrics, traces, and logs in a vendor-neutral format, and you can export them to any backend, Prometheus, Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, Datadog, by changing configuration, not application code. It is the "build-once, deploy-many" idea from W17, applied to telemetry: instrument once, send anywhere.

## The collector, and why it is the useful piece
OTel's other half is the collector, an agent (a sidecar, or a cluster-wide deployment) that receives telemetry from your apps and routes it to backends. Your app sends its spans and metrics to the local collector; the collector batches, processes, and forwards them to Tempo, Prometheus, or wherever. This decoupling is what makes the "switch backends without touching code" promise real, your app only knows about the collector, and the collector's config decides where the data goes. It also lets you do cross-cutting work (sampling, scrubbing sensitive fields, adding metadata) in one place instead of in every service.

## Why this matters beyond avoiding lock-in
OpenTelemetry is now the industry standard, CNCF-backed and supported by essentially every observability vendor, so learning it is learning the lingua franca rather than one company's dialect. The deeper value is that it unifies the three pillars under one SDK and one wire format: the same instrumentation produces the traces, the metrics, and the structured logs, with shared context (a trace ID that ties a span to its logs). That shared context is what makes the metric-to-trace-to-logs workflow actually connect, rather than being three tools that happen to be open at once. Instrumenting with OTel is how you get that integration for free instead of wiring it together by hand.

## Where this fits
Instrument your app with the OpenTelemetry SDK and send its telemetry through an OTel collector to your Prometheus and Tempo backends. Your observability is now vendor-neutral and unified, and you have done it the way the industry actually does it, which is both a portable skill and the thing that makes the three pillars work together rather than in isolation.

items.title: RED method (Tom Wilkie)
items.body:
## What to actually measure, so you are not drowning
Prometheus will happily collect thousands of metrics, and that is its own failure mode: a dashboard with a hundred panels tells you nothing because you cannot see the signal. The RED method (named by Tom Wilkie) is the cure, a tiny, opinionated set of metrics to track for every request-serving service:
- **Rate**, requests per second the service is handling.
- **Errors**, the rate of those requests that are failing.
- **Duration**, the distribution of how long requests take (latency, as percentiles).
Three numbers per service, and they capture almost everything you need to know about whether a request-handling service is healthy.

## Why these three, and not a hundred
RED works because the three answer the questions that actually matter to a user-facing service, in the order you ask them. Is it busy (Rate)? Is it failing (Errors)? Is it slow (Duration)? A spike in errors or a climb in p99 duration is what users feel, and what should wake someone up, while CPU and memory are causes you investigate after RED tells you something is wrong. Starting from RED keeps your dashboards and alerts focused on symptoms users experience rather than on the hundred internal metrics only useful once you are already diagnosing. (Its sibling, the USE method, Utilisation/Saturation/Errors, does the same job for resources like nodes and disks.)

## RED is how observability becomes alerting
This day is also the bridge to next week. RED metrics are exactly what you build SLOs on: "99.9% of requests succeed" is an Errors SLO, "p99 latency under 500ms" is a Duration SLO. Defining RED for your service is therefore the prerequisite for W20, you cannot set a reliability target on a number you do not measure, and RED is the small set of numbers worth targeting. Alert on RED symptoms (error rate up, latency up), not on every internal metric, and your on-call stops being a stream of noise nobody can act on.

## Where this fits
Build a focused RED dashboard for your Edge Portfolio, rate, error rate, and latency percentiles, on top of the Prometheus metrics you set up. This is the small, high-signal view you would actually keep on a screen, and it is the exact set of measurements W20 turns into formal SLOs and error budgets.

items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app can now be understood from the outside. By tonight:
- it exposes Prometheus metrics, scraped automatically, with a `kube-prometheus-stack` running on your cluster.
- Grafana shows a focused RED dashboard (rate, errors, duration) of its real behaviour.
- you can follow a single request as a distributed trace in Tempo, instrumented via OpenTelemetry.
- you can move metric to trace to logs to diagnose a problem, instead of guessing.

## The test that proves it
Break something on purpose and catch it through your tooling, not your code editor. Deploy a version that errors on some requests or adds artificial latency, then sit in front of your dashboards: the RED panel should show the error rate or p99 climbing within seconds. Open a trace of a slow request and confirm it points at the span you sabotaged, then read that service's logs at that timestamp. If your observability stack lets you find the fault you planted, without looking at the code that caused it, it works, and that is the exact muscle you will use on a real incident you did not plant.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the observability config, the OTel instrumentation, the Prometheus scrape setup, and the Grafana dashboard definitions as code (dashboards are JSON you can version), with a README on what each RED panel means and how to read a trace. Dashboards-as-code matters: a dashboard that lives only in someone's Grafana is lost when they leave, one in git is reproducible. This is a strong portfolio piece because observability is where many engineers are weakest, demonstrating you can instrument and diagnose a system, not just deploy it, is a real differentiator.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now see what your system is doing and diagnose why when it misbehaves, the foundation the rest of the operating phase requires. Next week (SRE) takes the RED metrics you are now collecting and turns them into formal reliability targets, SLOs and error budgets, that drive real engineering decisions. You cannot manage reliability you cannot measure; this week is where you started measuring it.

weeks.title: SRE, SLOs, Error Budgets, On-Call
weeks.context:
Site Reliability Engineering is the discipline of applying software engineering to infrastructure and operations problems. It originated at Google when they hired software engineers to run production systems and gave them the mandate to automate themselves out of operational toil. The result: Google runs millions of servers with a small SRE team. The SRE book (available free at sre.google) codifies these practices.

SLOs (Service Level Objectives): a target reliability level agreed upon between the SRE team and the product team. An SLO is not a promise to customers (that is an SLA, Service Level Agreement); it is an internal target used to make engineering decisions. Example: "The user-facing API will have 99.9% availability and p99 latency below 500ms, measured over a rolling 28-day window." SLOs are expressed in terms users experience, not infrastructure metrics.

Error budgets: the flip side of the SLO. If your SLO is 99.9% availability, your error budget is 0.1%, 43.8 minutes per month. Every minute of downtime spends error budget. When the error budget is exhausted, the SRE team can freeze new deployments (risk of more downtime) until the budget replenishes. This creates a shared incentive: developers want to ship fast, SREs want to maintain reliability. The error budget is the negotiation currency, if the budget is healthy, ship faster; if it is depleted, slow down and fix reliability.

Toil is work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and has no enduring value. Responding to the same alert every week and fixing it the same way is toil. Automating the alert response is engineering. Google's SRE teams have a rule: no more than 50% of time spent on toil. The other 50% is engineering work that reduces future toil. This ratio is what makes SRE scalable.

On-call best practices. Alerts must be actionable, if an alert fires and you cannot do anything about it, it should not be an alert. Alerts must have runbooks, documented steps for the on-call engineer. Incidents must be reviewed, post-incident reviews (PIRs, also called post-mortems) are blameless analyses of what happened, why, and what systemic changes prevent recurrence. Blameless means the root cause is a system design issue, not individual failure.

Chaos engineering (from W10's stretch) is the SRE practice of deliberately introducing failures to discover system weaknesses before they cause outages. Failure injection in production (with careful controls) builds confidence that your reliability mechanisms actually work.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Last week you learned to see your system. This week you learn to set targets for it and run it like the discipline that does this at scale: Site Reliability Engineering. SRE is software engineering applied to operations, it started at Google when they put software engineers in charge of running production and told them to automate their way out of manual toil. The practices you build this week, service-level objectives, error budgets, blameless post-mortems, sane on-call, are how a small team keeps a large system reliable without burning out. By Sunday your Edge Portfolio has a defined SLO, an error budget, and the alerting and review practices that make reliability a measured thing rather than a vibe.

## Why reliability needs a number, not a feeling
"The site should be reliable" is useless as a target, because it has no number to decide against. SRE's core move is to make reliability concrete: pick a measurable target (99.9% of requests succeed over 28 days), and use it to make engineering decisions. That single shift, from "be reliable" to "hit this number," changes everything downstream: it tells you when to stop shipping features and fix stability, what to alert on, and how to have a non-emotional conversation between developers who want to ship and operators who want stability. The number is the tool; this week is about choosing it and using it.

## The big idea: 100% is the wrong target
The most counterintuitive and most important SRE idea: you should not aim for 100% reliability. Chasing the last fraction of a percent costs enormous effort, and users cannot even tell the difference (their own network and devices fail more often than a well-run 99.9% service). So you pick a target that is good enough for users, and you deliberately spend the gap below 100%, the error budget, on shipping features and taking risks. Reliability stops being "as high as possible" and becomes "exactly as high as users need, and no higher," which frees the rest of the budget for moving fast. That reframing is the heart of the whole week.

## Where this fits
You define an SLO for your app from last week's RED metrics, derive its error budget, and set up the alerting and post-incident practices around it. This is the capstone of the operating phase's "run it well" arc, and it is the language (SLOs, error budgets, toil, blameless reviews) that every infrastructure and SRE interview expects you to speak.

items.title: SLIs, SLOs, SLAs
items.body:
## Three acronyms, one ladder
These three are constantly confused, and untangling them is the foundation of everything else:
- An **SLI** (Service Level Indicator) is a measurement of how the service is doing, a number, usually from your RED metrics. "The fraction of requests that succeed." "The fraction served under 500ms."
- An **SLO** (Service Level Objective) is a target for an SLI. "99.9% of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 28 days." It is internal; it is what you engineer against.
- An **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) is a contract with customers that includes consequences (refunds, credits) if you miss it. It is external and legal.
The ladder: you measure an SLI, you target it with an SLO, and only sometimes do you promise a looser version of it to customers as an SLA.

## Why your SLO should be stricter than your SLA
A deliberate gap belongs between your internal SLO and any external SLA, and it is a safety margin, not redundancy. If you promise customers 99.9% (the SLA) but target 99.95% internally (the SLO), you start fixing reliability when you breach the internal target, well before you breach the contract and owe refunds. The SLO is the alarm; the SLA is the wall you must not hit. Setting them equal means your first warning is the breach that costs you money. This is why mature teams treat the SLO as the thing they actually manage to, and the SLA as a looser promise with margin to spare.

## Express SLOs in what users feel
The discipline that makes an SLO useful: state it in terms users experience, not infrastructure internals. "99.9% of API requests succeed and 99% complete under 500ms" is a user-facing SLO, it describes what a person interacts with. "CPU stays under 80%" is not an SLO, it is an internal metric that may or may not correlate with anyone's experience (a service can be at 30% CPU and completely broken). The test is: would a user notice if this number got worse? If yes, it is a candidate SLO; if no, it is a diagnostic metric for after an SLO has already told you something is wrong. Availability and latency, your RED Errors and Duration, are the classic user-facing SLIs for exactly this reason.

## Where this fits
Define one or two real SLOs for your Edge Portfolio from last week's RED metrics, an availability target and a latency target, stated as a user would feel them, over a rolling window. You now have the measurable reliability target the rest of the week operates on, including the error budget you derive from it tomorrow.

items.title: Burn-rate alerts
items.body:
## The error budget, derived
Yesterday's SLO has an immediate consequence: its inverse is your error budget, the amount of failure you are allowed. A 99.9% availability SLO means 0.1% of requests may fail, which over a month is about 43 minutes of full downtime (or its equivalent spread across many small failures). That budget is a real, spendable quantity. Every error, every minute of downtime, spends it. When it is healthy, you have room to ship risky changes and move fast; when it is exhausted, the SRE convention is to freeze risky deploys and spend effort on reliability until the budget replenishes over the rolling window. The error budget is the shared currency between "ship features" and "stay reliable", a depleted budget is the objective signal to slow down.

## Why alert on burn rate, not on every blip
The naive approach, alert whenever any error happens, produces noise nobody can act on and trains people to ignore alerts. The SRE approach alerts on burn rate: how fast you are consuming the error budget relative to the window. A small, steady trickle of errors that will not threaten the monthly budget does not need to wake anyone, while a spike burning the whole month's budget in an hour absolutely does. Burn-rate alerting ties the alarm to the thing that actually matters (am I going to miss my SLO?) rather than to raw error counts, so the alerts that fire are the ones worth being woken for.
```promql
# fast burn: error budget being consumed ~14x too fast over 1h -> page now
( 1 - ( sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[1h]))
        / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h])) ) ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
```

## The two-speed alert pattern
The mature setup uses multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts, two speeds. A fast-burn alert (budget disappearing in hours) pages someone immediately, because at that rate you will blow the SLO today. A slow-burn alert (budget eroding over days) opens a ticket rather than paging, because it is a real problem but not a 3am one. This two-speed design solves the central alerting tension: page for the genuine emergencies, ticket for the slow problems, and stay quiet for the noise. It is the difference between an on-call rotation people can sustain and one that burns engineers out in a month.

## Where this fits
Compute your app's error budget from its SLO, and configure a fast-burn page and a slow-burn ticket in Alertmanager. Your alerting is now tied to reliability you actually promised yourself, not to raw error counts, which is the single biggest lever for an on-call that is both effective and humane, the subject you build out across the rest of the week.

items.title: Blameless post-mortems
items.body:
## The point is the system, not the person
When an incident happens, the instinct is to find who broke it. SRE deliberately rejects that, and the reason is practical, not just kind. A blameless post-mortem (or PIR, post-incident review) analyses what happened, why, and what systemic change prevents recurrence, treating the root cause as a flaw in the system, not a failure of the person who tripped over it. The logic: if a junior engineer running one command could take down production, the real defect is a system that allowed one command to do that, not the engineer. Blame the person and you fix nothing and teach everyone to hide mistakes; fix the system and that class of incident stops happening.

## Why blame is technically counterproductive
Blameless is not soft, it is the only approach that actually improves reliability, and here is the mechanism. The moment post-mortems assign blame, people stop being honest in them, they minimise, omit, and defend, because admitting "I ran the wrong command" now has a personal cost. You lose the truthful account that is the entire point of the exercise. A blameless culture gets you the real timeline and the real contributing factors, because nobody is protecting themselves, and only a truthful account lets you find the systemic fixes (a missing guardrail, a confusing UI, an alert that fired too late). You are trading the satisfaction of blame for the information that prevents recurrence.

## What a good post-mortem produces
A post-mortem is judged by its action items, not its narrative. A good one yields concrete, owned, systemic changes: "add a confirmation prompt to the deletion command," "alert on the condition we missed," "add a guardrail that makes this mistake impossible." Vague outcomes ("be more careful," "communicate better") are the tell of a review that found a scapegoat instead of a cause, you cannot assign "be more careful" to anyone or verify it is done. The questions that drive good action items: what made this possible, what made it hard to detect, what made it hard to recover, and what specific change addresses each. Each answer should become a tracked task with an owner.

## Where this fits
Write a short blameless post-mortem for a real or imagined incident on your Edge Portfolio (the broken deploy you caught in W19 is a perfect candidate), with a timeline, contributing factors, and concrete action items, no names attached to blame. You are practising the single most important cultural artifact in reliability work, the one that turns an outage from a bad day into a permanent improvement, and it is something interviewers genuinely probe for.

items.title: On-call rotations
items.body:
## Make on-call sustainable, or lose your engineers
Someone has to be reachable when the system breaks, and how you run that rotation determines whether your team stays or burns out. The core principles are about humaneness and effectiveness at once. Alerts must be actionable, if it fires and the on-call person can do nothing about it, it should not page; it should be a dashboard or a ticket. Every alert needs a runbook, documented steps so the person woken at 3am is not also reverse-engineering the system half-asleep. And the rotation must be sustainable, enough people that no one is permanently on the hook, with comp time or pay for the burden, because an on-call that wrecks people's lives loses the people.

## The two things that ruin on-call
Two failure modes destroy a rotation, and both are fixable. Alert fatigue: too many alerts, most of them noise, so the on-call engineer learns to ignore them, and then misses the real one. The fix is the discipline from D3, page only on actionable, budget-threatening conditions; everything else is a ticket. Hero culture: one person who knows everything carries every incident, which feels efficient until they leave or break. The fix is spreading knowledge through runbooks and rotation so any on-call engineer can handle the common incidents, not just the hero. A good rotation is deliberately designed so the system, not a person, is what makes incidents survivable.

## On-call is a feedback loop, not just firefighting
The deepest point: a healthy on-call rotation is a signal about your system's quality, and you should treat it as one. If the same alert fires every week and is fixed the same way, that is toil, manual repetitive work with no lasting value, and SRE's rule is that toil should be engineered away, not endured (Google's teams cap toil at 50% of time so the other half can reduce future toil). Every recurring page is a backlog item: automate the fix, add the missing guardrail, tune the bad alert. Run this way and on-call gets quieter over time because the system gets better; run it as pure firefighting and it stays loud forever. The rotation is how you find the work that makes the rotation lighter.

## Where this fits
Write a one-page on-call setup for your project: which conditions page (from D3's burn-rate alerts), the runbook for each, and the principle that recurring pages become engineering tickets. You are designing the human side of reliability, and even as a solo learner the discipline matters, an alert without a runbook and a clear "is this actionable" test is exactly the alert that will not help you when it fires for real.

items.title: Capacity planning
items.body:
## Will it handle next month, and what will that cost
Reliability is not only about handling failures, it is about having enough capacity to handle load, before the load arrives. Capacity planning is the practice of making sure your system can serve expected demand (the normal growth, the predictable spike, the marketing launch) without falling over or overspending. It sits at the intersection of the reliability and cost threads of this track: too little capacity and you breach your SLO when traffic climbs; too much and you are paying (W21's concern) for idle headroom. The job is to provision for the load you will actually have, with a sane margin, and to know your numbers well enough to predict when you will need more.

## Headroom, autoscaling, and load testing
Three tools do the work, and you have met all of them. Autoscaling (W10's HPA, W14's Karpenter) handles dynamic demand, scaling pods and nodes with load, but it has limits: it reacts, so a sudden spike can outrun it, and it cannot conjure capacity a quota or a cluster ceiling forbids. Headroom is the deliberate buffer you keep above normal load so a spike does not immediately breach the SLO while autoscaling catches up. Load testing is how you find your real limits before users do: drive synthetic traffic at the system, watch where latency degrades and what breaks first, and you learn the actual ceiling instead of guessing. Knowing "we degrade at 2,000 requests per second" is worth more than any amount of hoping.

## Plan for the spike you can predict
The highest-value capacity work targets known events, because those are the failures you can prevent entirely. A product launch, a marketing campaign, Black Friday, a feature on a big site, these are predictable load spikes, and failing to plan for them is a self-inflicted outage. The practice: estimate the expected peak (often a multiple of normal traffic), confirm via load test that the system holds at that level with headroom, pre-scale if autoscaling alone will not react fast enough, and have a plan to shed load gracefully if you are wrong. An unplanned outage during your biggest traffic moment is the most expensive kind, and it is the one capacity planning specifically exists to prevent.

## Where this fits
Estimate your Edge Portfolio's capacity, run a small load test to find where it degrades, and write down how it would handle 10x normal traffic (what autoscales, where the ceiling is, what you would pre-scale for a known spike). You are closing the reliability loop, you can now see the system (W19), target its reliability (this week), AND ensure it has the capacity to hit that target under load, which is exactly the foresight that separates running a system from merely deploying one.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your app is now run, not just deployed. By tonight:
- it has one or two real SLOs (availability and latency) stated in user-facing terms over a rolling window, built on W19's RED metrics.
- its error budget is computed, and you have fast-burn (page) and slow-burn (ticket) alerts tied to it.
- you have written a blameless post-mortem for an incident, ending in concrete, owned action items.
- you have an on-call and capacity plan: runbooks, the actionable-alert test, and a known load ceiling.

## The test that proves it
This week's proof is a decision, made with the numbers. Take your error budget and answer, concretely: given the current budget, should you ship a risky change this week or freeze and fix reliability? If the budget is healthy, ship; if a recent incident burned most of it, freeze, and be able to say exactly why from the number. Being able to make that call from the error budget, rather than from gut feel or whoever argues loudest, is the entire point of SRE, it turns "should we ship or stabilise?" from an argument into a reading off a dashboard. That is the deliverable: reliability as a managed quantity.

## Ship the artifact
Document the reliability setup in a `docs/sre.md`: the SLOs and why those targets, the error budget and the freeze policy, the alerting (fast-burn vs slow-burn), the on-call runbooks, and a sample post-mortem. This is one of the strongest portfolio artifacts on the whole track, because SRE thinking is rare and senior, an engineer who can define an SLO, derive an error budget, alert on burn rate, and run a blameless post-mortem is demonstrating exactly the judgement infrastructure and SRE roles hire for. It shows you can run a system responsibly, not just stand one up.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now see your system, set measurable reliability targets, alert on what matters, review incidents to make the system better, and plan capacity for the load ahead. That is the operating discipline, and it completes the "run it well" arc. The last operational concerns are cost (W21, controlling what all this infrastructure spends) and disaster recovery (W22, surviving the failures even good reliability cannot prevent), after which the track turns to security and the capstone. You have learned to build, ship, and now run; the remaining weeks are about doing all three economically and resiliently.

weeks.title: Cost Optimisation, FinOps and the AWS Bill
weeks.context:
Cloud bills grow in proportion to how little you pay attention to them. The discipline of managing cloud costs is called FinOps (Financial Operations). Most teams over-provision infrastructure by 30-50% "just in case" and then forget about it. A FinOps practice makes cost visible, allocates it to teams, and creates incentives to optimise.

The biggest cost levers in AWS (and broadly applicable): right-sizing instances (running a c5.4xlarge when a c5.xlarge handles the load), Reserved Instances or Savings Plans (committing to 1-3 years of a certain capacity for 30-60% savings), spot instances (unused AWS capacity at 70-90% discount, interruptible, suitable for batch jobs, CI runners, stateless workloads), NAT Gateway data processing ($0.045/GB processed, a hidden cost driver), EBS snapshots and unused volumes, data transfer costs (egress from AWS to the internet), and idle resources (development environments left running on weekends).

AWS Cost Explorer is your primary cost analysis tool. It shows cost by service, by region, by tag (if you have resource tagging), by linked account (if you have AWS Organizations), and over time. The Cost Anomaly Detection feature alerts you when spend deviates significantly from the baseline, catching accidental expensive resources within hours instead of at the monthly bill.

Resource tagging is the foundation of cost allocation. Without tags, you cannot determine which team, product, or environment is responsible for which costs. Define a tagging taxonomy before creating resources: Environment (prod/staging/dev), Team (infrastructure/frontend/data), Product (app/analytics). Enforce tags with AWS Config rules or SCPs (Service Control Policies) that deny resource creation without required tags.

Kubernetes cost allocation: a Kubernetes cluster pools resources across many workloads. OpenCost (open source) and Kubecost track per-namespace and per-deployment costs by combining Kubernetes resource requests with cloud instance pricing. This answers: "how much does the payments service cost per month to run?"

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You have built real cloud infrastructure, an EKS cluster, load balancers, storage, a NAT gateway, and real cloud infrastructure has a real bill. This week you learn to see that bill, understand what drives it, and bring it down without breaking anything. The discipline is FinOps (financial operations): make cost visible, attribute it to who incurred it, and build the habits that keep it from creeping. By Sunday you can read your AWS bill by service and by tag, you have a budget alarm that warns you before a surprise, and you have applied the big cost levers (right-sizing, commitment discounts, storage tiers) to your own stack.

## Why cost is an engineering problem, not just finance's
Cloud bills grow in proportion to how little attention you pay them, and most teams over-provision by 30 to 50% "just in case" and then forget. That waste is an engineering problem because engineers create it (an oversized instance, a volume nobody deleted, a dev environment left running all weekend) and only engineers can fix it. FinOps treats cost as a first-class engineering metric, the same as latency or reliability, something you measure, attribute, and optimise, rather than a number finance complains about after the fact. The skill is real and increasingly demanded: an engineer who can cut a cloud bill 30% without hurting reliability is directly valuable.

## The shape of where the money goes
A useful map before the details: in a typical AWS setup the big costs are compute (your EKS nodes, the largest line), then data transfer (egress and cross-AZ, the sneaky one), then storage (EBS, S3, snapshots), then managed-service fees and the small-but-constant items (the NAT gateway processing every gigabyte, idle load balancers). The 80/20 of cost optimisation lives in a few places: right-size the compute, commit to the baseline you always run for a discount, tier your storage, and kill what is idle. Knowing the shape tells you where to look first, you do not optimise a $5 line while a $500 over-provisioned node group sits untouched.

## Where this fits
You make your Edge Portfolio stack's cost visible and apply the main levers to it this week. This connects to everything you have built, the autoscaling from W14, the storage from W10, the multi-tenancy from W14 are all cost levers, and it sets up the final operating concern, surviving disasters (W22), economically.

items.title: AWS Cost Explorer + budgets
items.body:
## You cannot optimise what you cannot see
The first move in FinOps is always visibility, and on AWS that is Cost Explorer. It breaks your spend down by service, by region, by linked account, over time, so "the bill is high" becomes "EC2 in us-east-1 is 60% of it, and it jumped last Tuesday." That specificity is the whole point: optimisation is impossible while cost is one opaque monthly number, and trivial once you can see which service, which day, which resource is driving it. Spend your first session here, just reading your own bill until you understand its shape, because every later lever is aimed by what you see in Cost Explorer.

## Tags are what make cost answerable
Cost Explorer can only slice cost by the dimensions your resources are tagged with, which makes resource tagging the unglamorous foundation of all cost allocation. Without tags, you can see "EC2 costs $400" but not "the analytics team's staging environment costs $400", and you cannot fix what you cannot attribute. Define a tagging taxonomy before you create resources, the usual axes are `Environment` (prod/staging/dev), `Team`, and `Product`, and enforce it so untagged resources cannot be created (AWS Config rules, or an SCP that denies creation without required tags). Tagging feels like bureaucracy until the first time someone asks "why did the bill go up," and tags turn that from an investigation into a query.

## Budgets and anomaly detection: catch it in hours, not at month-end
Visibility after the fact is not enough; you want to know about a cost problem when it starts, not when the invoice arrives. Two AWS features do this. A Budget sets a threshold and emails you when actual or forecasted spend crosses it (the same idea as W1's $5 billing alarm, now grown up). Cost Anomaly Detection learns your normal spend pattern and alerts when spend deviates sharply, catching the accidentally-launched expensive resource or the runaway job within hours instead of at the monthly bill. The difference is stark: a misconfigured resource caught on day one costs a few dollars; the same resource discovered at month-end has run up thirty days of charges.

## Where this fits
Open Cost Explorer on your own account, confirm your resources are tagged with at least Environment and Team, and set a budget alert plus anomaly detection. You now have the visibility layer every other lever this week depends on, you can see where your money goes, attribute it, and get warned before a surprise becomes a bill.

items.title: Right-sizing
items.body:
## The biggest, most boring lever
The single largest source of cloud waste is the least exciting to fix: right-sizing, running instances and resource requests that match actual usage instead of a guess made "to be safe." Teams routinely run a `c5.4xlarge` where a `c5.xlarge` would handle the load, or set Kubernetes resource requests at triple what a pod ever uses, and pay for the gap every hour forever. Right-sizing is just closing that gap: measure what the workload actually uses, and provision close to it with a sane margin. It is unglamorous and it is usually the biggest single win on the bill, which is exactly why it gets neglected.

## Measure, do not guess
You cannot right-size from intuition; you size from data, and you already built the tools to get it. AWS Compute Optimizer analyses your instances' real utilisation and recommends a smaller type when one is over-provisioned. For Kubernetes, the metrics from W19 (`kubectl top`, the Prometheus data) show what pods actually consume, so you can set resource requests near real steady-state usage instead of the inflated number someone copied from a tutorial. The W10 lesson on requests and limits pays off here: requests that match reality let the scheduler pack pods efficiently and stop you paying for reserved-but-idle capacity, while requests set "to be safe" silently waste a chunk of every node.

## Right-size, then let autoscaling handle the rest
Right-sizing is not a one-time cut; it pairs with the autoscaling you already set up. The combined discipline: size each workload to its real steady-state need, then let HPA and Karpenter (W14) flex capacity for the peaks, so you are neither over-provisioned at baseline nor falling over at the spike. The anti-pattern is provisioning for peak load permanently, paying for Black-Friday capacity every ordinary Tuesday, which right-sizing-plus-autoscaling specifically eliminates. There is also a floor to respect: do not right-size so aggressively that you breach the SLO or leave no headroom, the goal is matching real demand with margin, not shaving until the service is fragile.

## Where this fits
Look at your own cluster's utilisation, find one over-provisioned thing (an oversized node type, an inflated resource request), and right-size it, then confirm autoscaling still handles load. You have pulled the biggest cost lever, and connected the reliability tools (metrics, autoscaling, requests/limits) you already built to the cost goal they were quietly serving all along.

items.title: Think it through
items.body: Reserved Instances vs Savings Plans, which gives more flexibility? Which gives more discount?

items.title: Savings plans + reserved instances
items.body:
## Pay less for the capacity you always run
Right-sizing fixed how much you run; this lever fixes how much you pay for it. By default you pay on-demand prices, the flexible, most-expensive rate. But most workloads have a baseline that runs 24/7, and for that steady floor AWS will give you a large discount (30 to 60%) in exchange for a commitment. Two instruments: Reserved Instances (commit to a specific instance type for 1 or 3 years) and the more flexible Savings Plans (commit to a dollar-per-hour of compute spend for 1 or 3 years, and AWS applies the discount across whatever instances you run). The logic is simple: you are always running some baseline anyway, so paying on-demand rates for it is leaving 30 to 60% on the table.

## Commit to the floor, stay flexible above it
The strategy that gets the discount without the trap: commit only to your stable baseline, the capacity you are confident you will run for the whole term, and cover everything above that with on-demand and spot. Commit too little and you miss savings on capacity you obviously needed; commit too much and you are locked into paying for instances you no longer use (a real way to waste money in the name of saving it). Savings Plans are usually the better default for exactly this reason: their flexibility means a commitment to "$X/hour of compute" keeps applying even as you change instance types, so you are committing to a spend level you are sure of, not a specific machine you might outgrow.

## Layer the pricing models
The mature cost setup uses all three purchasing modes together, each for the right slice of demand. Reserved/Savings Plans for the always-on baseline (steady, predictable, so commit and save). On-demand for the variable middle that autoscaling adds and removes (flexible, no commitment, worth the premium for not being locked in). Spot (W14's Karpenter lever) for interruption-tolerant work (CI runners, batch jobs, stateless replicas) at a steep discount. Picture demand as a stack: a committed-discount floor, an on-demand band that flexes with traffic, and spot capacity for the tolerant workloads. Matching each layer of demand to the cheapest pricing model that fits it is most of advanced cost optimisation.

## Where this fits
Estimate your stack's stable baseline (the compute you run every hour regardless of traffic) and reason about what a Savings Plan on that floor would save, while leaving variable capacity on-demand and tolerant work on spot. You have learned to pay the right price for each kind of demand, which together with right-sizing is where the largest, most durable cost reductions actually come from.

items.body: S3 storage class lifecycle, when does Glacier Deep Archive actually pay off? At what access frequency?

items.title: S3 storage classes
items.body:
## Not all stored data deserves the same price
Compute is the biggest bill, but storage quietly accumulates, and S3 gives you a lever most people ignore: storage classes, different price-and-access tiers for the same bucket. The default, S3 Standard, is priced for data you access often. But a lot of stored data is not accessed often, last quarter's logs, old backups, raw data you keep for compliance, and paying Standard prices to store it is waste. The cheaper tiers trade retrieval speed and cost for much lower storage cost: Standard-IA (infrequent access) for data you rarely touch, Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive for archives you might need once a year, at a tiny fraction of Standard's price.

## Lifecycle policies move data down the tiers automatically
You do not re-tier data by hand; you set a lifecycle policy that ages it down automatically. A typical rule: keep objects in Standard for 30 days (while they are likely to be accessed), transition to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier after 90, and expire (delete) after a retention period. The policy runs itself, so data flows to the cheapest appropriate tier as it ages without anyone remembering to move it.
```text
logs/  ->  Standard (0-30d)  ->  Standard-IA (30-90d)  ->  Glacier (90d+)  ->  delete (1y)
```
The savings are real because storage costs accrue forever, a bucket of old data on Standard costs many times what the same data costs on Glacier, every month, indefinitely.

## Match the tier to the access pattern, and mind retrieval
The discipline is to match each dataset's storage class to how you actually use it, with one caveat to respect. Frequently-read data stays on Standard (the cheaper tiers charge more, and more slowly, to retrieve, so they are false economy for hot data). Rarely-read data belongs on IA or Glacier. The caveat is retrieval cost and latency: Glacier is cheap to store and expensive and slow to read (minutes to hours), so it is right for "I will probably never need this, but must keep it" and wrong for anything you query regularly. Get the match wrong in the cold direction and a "cheap" archive becomes expensive every time you read it; get it right and old data costs almost nothing to keep.

## Where this fits
Add a lifecycle policy to a bucket of yours that holds aging data (logs, backups, build artifacts), transitioning it to cheaper classes and expiring it on a schedule. You have pulled the main storage cost lever, and the principle, match the price tier to the real access pattern, generalises to every storage decision you will make.

items.title: Tools
items.body:
## The Kubernetes cost-attribution problem
There is a specific blind spot the AWS bill cannot fix on its own: a Kubernetes cluster pools many workloads onto shared nodes, so AWS bills you for the nodes but cannot tell you that the payments service costs $300/month and the analytics service costs $1,200. That per-workload breakdown is exactly what a team needs to make cost decisions, and it requires combining two things AWS does not combine for you: Kubernetes' knowledge of which pod requested what resources, and the cloud's instance pricing.

## OpenCost and Kubecost
Two tools fill that gap. OpenCost (open source, a CNCF project) and Kubecost (a product built on it) do exactly the join above: they take each workload's Kubernetes resource requests and usage, multiply by the underlying instance pricing, and report cost per namespace, per deployment, per label. Now "how much does this service cost to run" is a dashboard, not a guess. This is the cost equivalent of W19's observability, you instrument the cluster so cost becomes visible per-workload, which is the precondition for attributing it to teams and finding the expensive thing to optimise.

## Why per-workload cost changes behaviour
Making cost visible per team or per service is not just reporting; it changes incentives, which is the real FinOps win. When a team can see their own namespace's monthly cost, they optimise it, the same way making latency visible (W19) makes people fix latency. Cost that is invisible or pooled into one company-wide number is nobody's problem; cost attributed to the team that incurred it becomes that team's problem to manage, and that attribution is what turns FinOps from a central team nagging everyone into each team owning its own efficiency. The tooling exists to create that feedback loop: see your cost, own your cost, reduce your cost.

## Where this fits
Install OpenCost (or read how it works) and look at your cluster's cost broken down per namespace and deployment. You have closed the FinOps loop, visibility at the AWS level (Cost Explorer), the cluster level (OpenCost), and the levers to act on both, which is the full shape of running cloud infrastructure economically rather than just running it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
You can now see and control what your infrastructure costs. By tonight:
- you can read your AWS bill by service and by tag in Cost Explorer, and a budget alert plus anomaly detection warns you before a surprise.
- you have right-sized at least one over-provisioned resource using real utilisation data.
- you can reason about the right pricing model (committed/on-demand/spot) for each layer of demand, and about storage tiers for aging data.
- you can attribute cluster cost per workload (OpenCost).

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a concrete, defensible cost reduction. Take your own stack, find the waste, an oversized node, an inflated resource request, a bucket of old data on Standard, a dev environment running all weekend, and quantify what fixing it saves per month, then fix the easiest one. "I right-sized the node group from 3x c5.2xlarge to 3x c5.large based on 20% measured utilisation, saving roughly $X/month with no SLO impact" is the exact sentence a FinOps practice produces, and being able to write it, with the number and the reliability caveat, is the skill. A cut you cannot quantify or defend against reliability is not optimisation; it is guessing.

## Ship the artifact
Document the cost work in a `docs/finops.md`: your bill's shape (where the money goes), your tagging taxonomy, the budget and anomaly alerts, and a list of the optimisations you made or identified with their estimated savings. This is a genuinely differentiating portfolio piece, most engineers cannot read a cloud bill, let alone systematically reduce it, so demonstrating that you treat cost as an engineering metric, with visibility, attribution, and quantified wins, signals a maturity infrastructure roles value and few candidates show.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now build it, ship it, run it reliably, and run it economically. The last operational gap is resilience against catastrophe: when a region fails or someone drops the database, can you recover, and how fast? That is next week (Disaster Recovery), and it has its own cost dimension you are now equipped to reason about (a hot standby region is reliable and expensive; a backup-and-restore plan is cheaper and slower). After DR comes security and the capstone. Cost is not a constraint bolted on at the end; it is a property you now design for alongside reliability.

weeks.title: Disaster Recovery, Backups, Multi-Region, and Tested Restores
weeks.context:
Disaster recovery is about business continuity when things go catastrophically wrong: a region goes down, data gets corrupted, a database is accidentally dropped, ransomware encrypts your storage. Most teams have backup policies they have never tested. The only backup that matters is one you have verified can be restored in the required time window.

Two key metrics define your DR requirements. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): the maximum age of data you can afford to lose. If your RPO is 1 hour, your backup frequency must be at least hourly, you can lose at most 1 hour of data. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): the maximum acceptable duration of downtime. If your RTO is 4 hours, your recovery procedure must restore service within 4 hours. Both are business decisions that inform technical choices.

Backup strategies. Database backups: PostgreSQL full backup (pg_dump) + WAL (Write-Ahead Log) archiving allows point-in-time recovery (PITR), restore to any second in the archive window. RDS automated backups provide 35-day PITR. Restore testing: quarterly, actually restore from backup to a test environment and verify data integrity. Object storage: enable versioning and cross-region replication on S3 buckets that contain critical data. Kubernetes resources: use Velero to backup and restore Kubernetes resources and PersistentVolumes.

Multi-region active-passive: your primary region (us-east-1) serves all traffic. A secondary region (eu-west-1) has the infrastructure to serve traffic but is idle or serving only a fraction. In a primary region failure, DNS fails over to the secondary (Route 53 health checks + failover records). RTO is 5-15 minutes (DNS propagation time). The secondary region's database is a read replica that gets promoted to primary.

Multi-region active-active: both regions serve traffic simultaneously. Users in the US go to us-east-1; users in Europe go to eu-west-1. Each region has its own database. Data is replicated between regions (using CockroachDB, Cassandra, or synchronised PostgreSQL replicas). More complex and expensive, lower latency for geographically distributed users.

The disaster you have not planned for: what about accidental data deletion? A developer runs DELETE FROM users WHERE id > 0 (meant WHERE id = 123). PostgreSQL PITR can restore the database to 5 seconds before the query. But only if you have WAL archiving configured and the backup is available.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Everything so far assumed your infrastructure mostly works. This week assumes it does not: a region goes dark, a database gets corrupted, someone runs a `DELETE` without a `WHERE`, ransomware encrypts your storage. Disaster recovery is the discipline of surviving those events, business continuity when things go catastrophically wrong. By Sunday your Edge Portfolio has a backup strategy with defined recovery targets, you have actually tested a restore (the only kind that counts), and you have written a runbook for failing over to another region. The theme of the week is uncomfortable and essential: hope is not a recovery plan, and an untested backup is not a backup.

## The hard truth: most backups do not work
Here is the line that should change how you think about this: the only backup that matters is one you have verified you can restore, in the time you need, with the data intact. Most teams have backup policies they have never tested, and discover at the worst possible moment that the backup was incomplete, or corrupted, or takes twelve hours to restore when they needed it in one. A backup you have never restored is not a safety net; it is a belief. So the centre of this week is not "configure backups" (the easy part) but "prove the restore works" (the part everyone skips and regrets).

## The two numbers that define your plan
Disaster recovery is not one-size-fits-all; it is sized by two business decisions you make explicit. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you can afford to lose, which sets how often you back up. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long you can afford to be down, which sets how fast your recovery procedure must be. These two numbers drive every technical choice, an RPO of one hour means hourly backups; an RTO of fifteen minutes rules out "restore from a backup that takes four hours" and pushes you toward a warm standby. You will set these for your own app on Day 2, because you cannot design a recovery plan without first deciding what "recovered" means and how fast.

## Where this fits
You define your recovery targets, build and test backups for your database and cluster, and write a failover runbook this week. This is the resilience layer on top of everything you built, reliability (W20) keeps the system up under normal failures; disaster recovery is what saves you from the catastrophic ones reliability cannot prevent. It is also the last operating concern before the track turns to security and the capstone.

days.title: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) vs RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
days.summary: Focus: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) vs RPO (Recovery Point Objective)

items.title: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) vs RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
items.body:
## Two questions that size your entire plan
Before any backup tooling, you answer two business questions, and everything technical follows from them:
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** how much data can you afford to lose? If the answer is "at most one hour," your backups must run at least hourly, because a disaster can cost you everything since the last backup. RPO sets backup frequency.
- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** how long can you afford to be down? If the answer is "at most four hours," your recovery procedure must reliably restore service within four hours. RTO sets recovery speed, and therefore your whole DR architecture.

## Why these are business decisions, not technical ones
The temptation is to answer "zero" to both, lose no data, never be down, but that is a budget statement disguised as a requirement, because both numbers cost money to shrink. An RPO near zero means continuous replication (expensive); an RTO near zero means a hot standby running full-time (double the infrastructure). So RTO and RPO are negotiations between the business's tolerance for loss and downtime and what it will pay, and different systems get different answers. Your billing database might warrant RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes; a marketing site can tolerate RPO of a day and RTO of hours. Setting the same aggressive target for everything wastes money protecting things that did not need it.

## The numbers pick the architecture
The two objectives map directly onto the DR strategy you choose, cheapest-and-slowest to most-expensive-and-fastest:
- **Backup and restore** (high RTO/RPO, low cost): restore from backups when disaster strikes. Hours to recover, cheap to maintain.
- **Pilot light / warm standby** (medium): a minimal or scaled-down copy of the system in another region, ready to scale up. Minutes to recover, moderate cost.
- **Hot standby / active-active** (low RTO/RPO, high cost): a full second environment already running. Near-instant recovery, double the bill.
You do not pick the fanciest; you pick the cheapest strategy whose recovery speed meets the RTO and RPO the business actually requires. That match, requirement to architecture to cost, is the core DR design decision.

## Where this fits
Set explicit RTO and RPO numbers for your Edge Portfolio (be honest, not aspirational), and name which DR strategy those numbers imply. Every backup and failover choice the rest of the week makes is now anchored to a target, you are designing recovery to a requirement, not configuring backups and hoping they are enough.

items.title: Database backups
items.body:
## The database is the irreplaceable part
Most of your infrastructure is reproducible, you can rebuild the cluster from Terraform and redeploy the app from a chart. The data is the one thing you cannot regenerate, which makes database backup the heart of disaster recovery. Two layers give you real protection for PostgreSQL: a periodic full backup (`pg_dump`, a complete snapshot), plus WAL archiving (Write-Ahead Log), which streams every change so you can replay forward from a full backup to any point in time. Together they enable point-in-time recovery (PITR): restore to any second within your archive window, not just to the last nightly snapshot.

## Why point-in-time recovery is the feature that matters
PITR is what saves you from the disaster nobody plans for: not a region failure, but an oops. A developer runs `DELETE FROM users WHERE id > 0` meaning `WHERE id = 123`, and the table is gone. A nightly-snapshot-only backup loses everything since midnight; PITR restores the database to five seconds before the bad query, losing almost nothing. This is the single most common "we needed the backup" scenario in practice, human error far more than hardware failure, and only PITR (full backup plus WAL archiving) handles it well. It is also why "we take a nightly dump" is a weaker answer than it sounds: it bounds your data loss at up to a full day.

## Managed databases make this easier, not automatic
On a managed database the mechanics are largely handled, one more reason W14 leaned toward RDS over self-hosting your primary database. RDS automated backups give you PITR with up to 35 days of retention out of the box, you enable it and set the window. But "handled" is not "thought about": you still own the decisions, the retention period (does it cover how long until you would notice corruption?), whether backups are replicated to another region (a backup in only the failed region is no help), and, above all, whether you have actually tested restoring one. Managed backups remove the toil of running `pg_dump` on a cron; they do not remove your responsibility for the recovery plan.

## Where this fits
Confirm PITR is configured for your database (RDS automated backups, or `pg_dump` plus WAL archiving if self-managed) with a retention window that meets your RPO, and that the backups live somewhere the disaster would not also destroy. You have protected the one irreplaceable asset, and set up the day that actually matters, proving you can restore it.
