items.title: Application-level backup tools
items.body:
## Backing up Kubernetes itself
Your database has its own backup story; the cluster around it needs one too. In a GitOps world (W18) much of your cluster state is already reproducible from git, you can recreate Deployments, Services, and config by pointing Argo CD at the repo. But two things are not in git: the PersistentVolumes (the actual data on disk for stateful workloads) and any cluster state that drifted or was created outside git. Velero is the tool that backs those up: it snapshots Kubernetes resources and the contents of PersistentVolumes, storing them in object storage (S3) so you can restore a namespace, or a whole cluster, elsewhere.

## What Velero does that GitOps does not
It is worth being precise about the division of labour, because it is a common confusion. GitOps reproduces your declared desired state, the manifests, the config, the structure, by replaying git onto a fresh cluster. Velero captures runtime state, including the data in volumes and the actual live objects, which git does not contain. So they are complementary: rebuild the cluster's shape from git, restore its data and any non-declared state from Velero. For a fully GitOps-managed stateless app, git plus the database's own backups may be enough; the moment you have stateful workloads in-cluster (a database StatefulSet, a cache with persistence, uploaded files on a PV), Velero is what backs up the part git cannot.

## Restore is a migration tool, not just a panic button
Velero's quiet superpower is that "restore to a different cluster" is the same operation as "recover from disaster," which makes it useful well beyond catastrophe. The same backup-and-restore that saves you when a cluster dies also lets you migrate a namespace to a new cluster, clone production into a staging environment for realistic testing, or move between regions. Designing your cluster so it can be backed up and restored elsewhere is therefore not just DR insurance; it is the property that keeps the cluster from becoming a pet you can never move. A cluster you can Velero-restore onto fresh infrastructure is a cluster you actually control.

## Where this fits
Install Velero, back up your app's namespace (including any PersistentVolumes), and confirm the backup lands in S3. You now have the Kubernetes half of your backup story to go with the database half, and tomorrow you do the thing that turns both from theory into trust, you restore them and verify.

items.title: Tested restores
items.body:
## The backup you have never restored is not a backup
This is the most important day of the week, and the one teams skip. A backup is a belief until you have restored it; only a tested restore is a fact. The failure modes are many and silent: the backup was incomplete, it was corrupted, it covered the wrong data, the restore procedure has a missing step nobody documented, or it works but takes ten hours when your RTO is two. None of these show up while the backup sits in S3 looking healthy. They show up at the one moment you cannot afford them, during the actual disaster, which is precisely why the restore must be tested before then, on a normal Tuesday, with nothing on fire.

## What a real restore test looks like
A genuine test restores from backup into a separate environment and verifies two things: the data is intact, and the recovery fit inside your RTO. Concretely, take a recent backup, restore the database (and, with Velero, the cluster state) into a fresh test environment, then check data integrity (row counts, recent records present, referential integrity, can the app actually start against it) and time the whole thing. The timing matters as much as the data: discovering that your "four-hour RTO" restore actually takes nine hours is a finding you want now, not during an outage. Do this on a schedule, quarterly is a common cadence, because a restore that worked last quarter can break as the data and tooling change.

## Why this builds the thing you actually need: confidence
The deeper purpose of restore testing is not just catching broken backups; it is building justified confidence that you can recover. Before you have tested a restore, "we have backups" is a hope that collapses into panic during a real incident. After you have restored successfully and timed it, you know, with evidence, that you can bring the system back and roughly how long it takes, which transforms an incident from a frantic improvisation into the execution of a procedure you have already run. That calm-under-fire is the entire payoff: disasters are survivable not because nothing breaks, but because you have rehearsed the recovery and it is muscle memory, not a first attempt.

## Where this fits
Restore one of your backups (database, or the Velero cluster backup) into a test environment, verify the data is intact, and time how long it took against your RTO. You have done the single thing that separates a real DR plan from a theoretical one, and you can now say "we can recover" as a tested fact rather than a hope, which is the whole point of the week.

items.title: Runbook for region failover
items.body:
## When the whole region is gone
The largest disaster is an entire region failing, and you cannot improvise your way through it at 3am. The defence is a multi-region posture plus a written runbook. The common, affordable shape is active-passive: your primary region (say us-east-1) serves all traffic, while a secondary region (eu-west-1) holds standby infrastructure and a database read replica. When the primary fails, you fail over: DNS (Route 53 health checks and failover records) redirects traffic to the secondary, and the read replica is promoted to primary so it can accept writes. RTO is typically minutes (mostly DNS propagation), at a fraction of the cost of running two full active regions.

## Active-passive vs active-active
The two multi-region models trade cost against latency and complexity, and the right one depends on your RTO/RPO and your budget. Active-passive (above) keeps the standby idle or minimal until needed, cheaper, simpler, with a short-but-nonzero failover time. Active-active runs both regions serving traffic simultaneously (US users to us-east-1, EU users to eu-west-1), each with its own database and cross-region data replication, giving the lowest latency for a global user base and near-instant survival of a region loss, at the cost of real complexity (keeping two databases consistent across regions is genuinely hard) and roughly double the infrastructure. Most teams that need multi-region start active-passive, because it meets a strong RTO without the operational weight of active-active.

## The runbook is the deliverable, because failover is rare and high-stakes
Region failover is the definition of a procedure you execute rarely and cannot afford to get wrong, which is exactly the kind of thing that must be a written, tested runbook, not knowledge in one person's head. The runbook spells out the steps in order: confirm the primary is actually down (do not fail over on a false alarm), promote the read replica, switch DNS, verify the secondary is serving and healthy, and, critically, how to fail back once the primary recovers (often the harder direction, because data written to the secondary during the outage must be reconciled). Because you will run it under stress and infrequently, the runbook must assume a tired human and leave nothing to memory or judgement that can be written down instead.

## Where this fits
Write the region-failover runbook for your Edge Portfolio: the failover steps, the DNS and database-promotion specifics, the health checks that confirm success, and the fail-back procedure. Even if you do not stand up a full second region, the runbook is the artifact, it is what turns "the region is down" from a catastrophe into a procedure, and it is the capstone of treating recovery as something you plan and rehearse, not something you face cold.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your system can now survive the catastrophes, not just the routine failures. By tonight:
- you have explicit RTO and RPO targets, and a DR strategy matched to them.
- your database has point-in-time recovery; your cluster's stateful data is backed up with Velero.
- you have actually restored a backup into a test environment and timed it against your RTO.
- you have a written region-failover runbook, including how to fail back.

## The test that proves it
The proof of disaster recovery is, by its nature, a rehearsal, so rehearse the worst plausible case end to end. Simulate the data-loss disaster: in a test environment, "accidentally" corrupt or delete data, then recover it using point-in-time recovery to just before the damage, and verify the data is whole. Time it. If you can take a database from "a developer just dropped the users table" back to five seconds before the mistake, with the data intact, inside your RTO, your DR plan is real. The combination, a disaster injected and recovered from on purpose, with the clock running, is the only honest test, and it is the deliverable.

## Ship the artifact
Document the DR plan in a `docs/disaster-recovery.md`: the RTO and RPO targets and why, the backup strategy (database PITR, Velero), the evidence that you tested a restore (what you restored, that the data was intact, how long it took), and the region-failover runbook. This is a strong and unusual portfolio artifact, because tested DR is rare even at real companies; demonstrating that you do not just configure backups but verify recovery and document the procedure shows exactly the operational rigour that separates someone who can run production from someone who can only deploy to it.

## Where this fits in the track
The operating arc is now complete: you can see the system (W19), keep it reliable (W20), run it economically (W21), and recover it from catastrophe (W22). Your Edge Portfolio is built, shipped, observed, run to targets, cost-controlled, and disaster-resilient, which is genuinely the full lifecycle of production infrastructure. The remaining weeks turn to securing it properly (W23) and pulling everything together into the capstone (W24). You have learned to keep a system alive through the failures that take other systems down for good.

weeks.title: Cloud Security Posture, IAM, Network, Audit
weeks.context:
Cloud security posture is the aggregate security state of all your cloud resources. A misconfigured S3 bucket (public read on a bucket containing user data) has caused some of the largest data breaches in history. IAM misconfigurations (overly permissive roles, long-lived access keys, no MFA) are the leading cause of cloud account compromise. Network misconfigurations (security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports) expose services that should be internal.

IAM best practices. The principle of least privilege: every user, service, and application should have exactly the permissions they need, no more. Avoid the AdministratorAccess policy except for break-glass accounts. Use IAM Roles for services (not long-lived access keys). Enable MFA for all human users (especially root and admin accounts). Rotate access keys regularly (or use OIDC/IRSA to eliminate long-lived keys entirely). Use the IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources accessible from outside your account.

Security scanning tools. Prowler is a free, open-source tool that scans your AWS account against hundreds of CIS AWS Benchmark checks, NIST, SOC2, and other compliance frameworks. It checks IAM policies, S3 bucket permissions, CloudTrail logging, VPC configurations, encryption settings, and more. AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from Prowler, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Inspector, and other security tools into one dashboard.

Network security. Security groups: allow inbound traffic from specific CIDR blocks or other security groups, not 0.0.0.0/0. Bastion hosts and Systems Manager Session Manager for SSH access (no public SSH port open). VPC design: public subnets only for load balancers; private subnets for compute and databases. VPC Flow Logs for auditing network traffic. AWS WAF in front of public-facing applications.

CloudTrail: records every API call to AWS. Who created that S3 bucket? Who changed the security group rule? Who deleted the IAM user? CloudTrail has the answer. Enable CloudTrail in every region, enable log file integrity validation, and store logs in a separate account that production has no access to (so an attacker who compromises production cannot tamper with the audit trail).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Prowler finds that your RDS database is publicly accessible (rds:DBInstancePubliclyAccessible = true). What does this mean, what is the risk, and how do you fix it? Publicly accessible means the RDS instance has a public IP address and could receive connections from the internet (depending on the security group). Risk: if the security group allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0, anyone on the internet can attempt to connect to your database. Even with a strong password, this exposes you to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and CVE exploitation. Fix: modify the RDS instance to set PubliclyAccessible to false (removes the public IP). Move the database to a private subnet. Connect from your application via the VPC-internal hostname. If you need direct access for debugging, use a bastion host or AWS SSM Session Manager tunnel.

weeks.title: Capstone, Build and Operate Real Infrastructure
weeks.context:
This is the capstone week. The DevOps/Cloud track ends where most engineers are trying to get to: owning and operating real infrastructure that serves real users. Edge Portfolio has evolved from a manually managed server (W1) to a production-grade Kubernetes deployment with GitOps, observability, security scanning, and disaster recovery. This week you bring all the pieces together and document the architecture.

The capstone deliverable is not just a running system, it is a documented, reproducible, auditable infrastructure. Another engineer (your future self, a new team member, or a potential employer reviewing your portfolio) should be able to understand the architecture, reproduce it from scratch using your Terraform code, and operate it using your runbooks.

Architecture documentation: write an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for each significant technical choice you made. Why Kubernetes over a simpler deployment? Why Terraform over manual setup? Why Flux over Argo CD? ADRs capture the reasoning behind decisions so future engineers understand why things are the way they are, not just how they work.

The infrastructure is code: every resource is in Terraform, every Kubernetes deployment is in the gitops repository, every secret is in the secrets manager, every alert has a runbook. Nothing exists that is not documented. Nothing is configured manually in the cloud console.

Operational readiness: before calling a system "production-ready," define and verify: the system can survive a single node failure without downtime (tested), the system can be restored from backup within the RTO (tested), alerts fire when the system is degraded (tested by injecting failures), the on-call runbook is complete and tested, the cost is within budget and monitored, and the security posture has been assessed (Prowler scan, findings addressed).

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it

This is the capstone week. The DevOps/Cloud track ends where most engineers are trying to get to: owning and operating real infrastructure that serves real users. Edge Portfolio has evolved from a manually managed server (W1) to a production-grade Kubernetes deployment with GitOps, observability, security scanning, and disaster recovery. This week you bring all the pieces together and document the architecture.

The capstone deliverable is not just a running system, it is a documented, reproduc

## Key ideas
- Understand the concept before reaching for code.
- Build the smallest working example first.
- Commit early and often so each step is reversible.

cards.prompt: The fastest way to learn a new tool is to read the docs end-to-end before writing any code.
cards.whenRight: Right - building a tiny example first beats reading every page.
cards.whenWrong: Docs are a reference, not a tutorial. Code first, read second.

cards.prompt: Committing small checkpoints helps you debug regressions and review your own progress.
cards.whenRight: Exactly - tiny commits are a superpower.
cards.whenWrong: They really do help; `git revert` is one command away.

cards.prompt: Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow without understanding is a sustainable long-term strategy.
cards.whenRight: Correct - understanding the why is what makes you employable.
cards.whenWrong: Short-term it works; long-term it stalls you.

items.title: Finish and ship the week's project
items.body:
[WRITE] Build a Full Production Stack for One Real App. End-state: an app of your choice (your URL shortener works, or fork something popular) running on EKS via Terraform via Argo CD with: HTTPS at a real domain, full observability (Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo), backups + tested restore, secrets in Doppler/Secrets Manager, CI/CD on every PR. Public GitHub repo. Documented blog post about the stack. This is what 'I can operate cloud infrastructure' actually looks like.

Ship checklist:
 - It runs from a clean clone / fresh open, no "works on my machine" steps missing.
 - Commit it to your repo with a short README saying what it does and how to run it.
 - Tag or note this as your Week 24 deliverable so you can look back on it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A new engineer joins the team and needs to understand your entire infrastructure. What documentation do you provide, and how do they reproduce it from scratch? Documentation: a README explaining the overall architecture with a diagram, the technology decisions and why (ADRs), the list of required tools and versions, the bootstrapping procedure (how to create a new environment from scratch). Reproduction: terraform init && terraform apply (creates all cloud resources). flux bootstrap (installs GitOps). helm upgrade --install (installs monitoring stack). The engineer should be able to stand up a complete replica of the infrastructure by following the runbook. If they cannot, the documentation is incomplete.
